DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT
ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Description of business

Ryan Health Center, Inc. (the "Centet") d/b/a Morgan Health Center, owns and
operates a 120-bed nursing facility located in Johnston, Rhode Island.

The Center provides services to patients, principally from Rhode Island, with third-
party financial coverage (principally Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients
who are responsible for their own financial obligations.

Recently issued but not yet effective accounting pronouncements

Revenue recognition

In May 2014, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) issued Accounting
Standards Update ("ASU") No. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts with Customers
(Accounting Standards Codification ("ASC") Topic 606), as amended (commonly
referred to as "ASC 606"), which requires an entity to recognize revenue to depict the
transfer of promised goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the
consideration which the entity expects to be entitled to receive in exchange for those
goods or services. ASC 606 replaces most existing revenue recognition standards in
accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America (“U.S.
GAAP”), including industry-specific standards, when it becomes effective. For annual
reporting periods, this standard is effective for the Center on January 1, 2019, and for
interim periods within annual periods that begin one year later. The standard permits
the use of cither the retrospective or cumulative-effect transition method. The Center is
currently completing its initial assessment and evaluation of the impact that ASC 606
will have on the Center’s financial statements and related disclosures.

The Center expects to retrospectively adopt ASC 606 effective January 1, 2019. Asa
result, substantially all amounts previously reported as provision for losses on patient
services receivables will now be considered an implicit price concession and will be
recognized as a reduction of net patient service revenue. The adoption of ASC 606 will
also result in expanded disclosures that will enable the users of the financial statements
to better understand the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty, if any, of revenues and
cash flows arising from contracts with customers.

Statement of cash flows

In August 2016, the FASB issued ASU No. 2016-15, Statement of Cash Flows (Topic 230)
- Classification of Certain Cash Receipts and Cash Payments ("ASU 2016-15"), which provides
guidance on several cash flow classification issues. This new guidance is effective for
years beginning after December 15, 2018, with early adoption permitted. The Center is
evaluating the effect that ASU 2016-15 will have on its financial statements and related
disclosures.

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT
ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Use of estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP requires
management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of
assets and liabilities, and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the
financial statements, and the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the
reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates. The allowance for
doubtful accounts is a significant estimate used in the preparation of the accompanying
financial statements.

Cash and cash equivalents

The Center considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three
months or less to be cash equivalents. At December 31, 2018, the Center had no cash
equivalents.

‘The Center maintains cash balances at various financial institutions in accounts insured
by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC"). The Center monitors its
concentration of deposits by obtaining and evaluating bank ratings on a quarterly basis.
At December 31, 2018, the Center had $1,118,579 of deposits in excess of the FDIC-
insured limits.

Patient services receivables
Patient services receivables are stated at the amount the Center expects to collect.

Under Rhode Island General Law Title 40, Chapter 8, Section 6.1(b)(2) , Haman Services,
Medical Assistance, Provider Care During Pendency of Application, Uncompensated Care While
Determination is Overdue, upon the Center’s request, the State of Rhode Island (the
"State") is required to make payments to the Center for charges related to a patient that
the Center has determined should be eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed
application for Medicaid benefits filed with the State has been pending for 90 days or
more ("advance payments"); such advance payments may not be recovered, offset or
recouped by the State upon a subsequent determination by the State that the patient is
not eligible for Medicaid. Consequently, advance payments received by the Center prior
to the date the State has made a determination related to the patient’s eligibility for
Medicaid are offset against the patient services receivables included in the accompanying
balance sheet. Advance payments received by the Center related to Medicaid claims
subsequently approved and paid by the State are required to be repaid to the State
through an ongoing reconciliation process and, consequently, are reported within
current liabilities, third-party advances in the accompanying balance sheet. At
December 31, 2018, advance payments offset against patient services receivables totaled
$888,759.

Patient services receivables (continued)

The Center provides for probable uncollectible amounts through a charge to bad debt
expense and a credit to the allowance for doubtful accounts based on its assessment of
the current status of individual accounts. Balances that are still outstanding after the
Center has used reasonable collection efforts are written off through a charge to the
allowance for doubtful accounts and a credit to receivables. The Center does not obtain
collateral for amounts due. The allowance for doubtful accounts increased by
approximately $46,000 for the year ended December 31, 2018.

Approximately 33% and 3% of the Center’s patient services receivables is due from the
Rhode Island Medicaid and federal Medicare programs, respectively.

Fixed assets

Fixed assets are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is provided
using the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets, ranging from
4 years to 40 years. Depreciation expense totaled $109,584 for the year ended
December 31, 2018.

The Center evaluates long-lived assets held and used by the Center for impairment
whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the
asset may not be recoverable. An impairment loss is recognized if the sum of the
expected undiscounted future cash flows from the use and disposition of the asset is
Jess than its carrying amount. Generally, the amount of impairment loss is measured as
the difference between the carrying amount of the asset and the estimated fair value of
the asset. ‘The Center did not record an impairment loss during the year ended
December 31, 2018.

Debt issuance costs

Debt issuance costs are being amortized over the term of the related debt using the
straight-line method, which approximates the effective interest method,

Income taxes

The Center has elected to be taxed as an S Corporation under the Internal Revenue
Code. Accordingly, the shareholders include the income or loss of the Center on their
respective income tax returns. In accordance with ASC 740, Income Taxes, the Center
applies the “more likely than not” threshold to the recognition and derecognition of tax
positions for its financial statements. Management has evaluated the Center’s tax
positions and has concluded that there were no uncertain tax positions that qualified for
either recognition or disclosure in these financial statements.

result, there is at least a reasonable possibility that recorded estimates could change by a

review and interpretation exists. Compliance with such laws and regulations can be
subject to future government review and interpretation, as well as significant regulatory
action; failure to comply with such laws and regulations can result in fines, penalties and
exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid programs.

RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS

Management fee

The Center has a management agreement with Health Concepts, Ltd. (the "Home
Office"), a company owned by the Center’s shareholders, to provide home office
services, principally management services. The agreement expires in May 2032, unless
automatically renewed for an additional 15-year term in December 2031. The
management fee is subject to a maximum rate of 7% of net patient service revenue. In
2018, management fees totaled 6% of net patient service revenue and amounted to
$606,291 for the year ended December 31, 2018.

Workers’ compensation insurance

Effective January 1, 1994, the Home Office received permission from the Rhode Island
Department of Labor to establish a pooled self-insured workers’ compensation plan (the
"Plan"). ‘The Home Office, the Center and eight nursing facilities owned by the
Center's shareholders participate in the Plan and have transferred their workers!
compensation insurance to the Plan.

The Plan provides for the payment of administration, claims and risk management
costs, as well as payment for losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions
(premium payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workers’ Compensation
Trust (the "Trust") through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to
establish a cumulative reserve for futute claims. The reserve is held in trust and invested
by the Plan trustee. The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a
commercial insurance carrier to protect the Trust's assets from individual losses in
excess of $450,000. In addition, the Trust carries a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode
Island Department of Labor, collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a
bank, for which no amounts are outstanding at December 31, 2018.

The Trust Committee (the "Committee") maintains separate accountability for each
participant’s portion of contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for
future claims. Should any participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims,
costs, and losses, the remaining participants’ portion of Trust assets can be used to
satisfy the payments allocated to that participant. In the event of Plan termination, any
assets remaining in the Trust in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and
losses will ultimately be returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares.

In the opinion of the Committee, the Plan has sufficient assets to mect a significant
portion of current and estimated future costs, losses and future claims; accordingly, the
Center's required premium for the year ended December 31, 2018, totaled $170,872, an
amount that, in management's opinion, is below the premium it would pay to a
commercial insurance carrier if the Plan did not exist and did not achieve significant
savings as a result of the loss control program and monitoring services provided by the
Home Office.

The Plan's net assets at December 31, 2018, include cash and investments with a cost,
which approximates fair value, of $922,700 (unaudited).

Health insurance

Effective January 1, 2018, the Home Office established a self-insured health insurance
plan (the "Health Plan"). ‘fhe Home Office, the Center and other nursing facilities and
a business owned by the Center's shareholders participate in the Health Plan and have
transferred their health insurance to the Health Plan. The Health Plan provides for the
payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as well as payment for
losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium payments), as required,
to the Health Pian account maintained at the Home Office to pay current costs and
losses and to establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The Health Plan carries
excess loss insurance coverage with a commercial insurance cartier to protect the Health
Plan's assets from individual losses in excess of $100,000.

The Home Office maintains separate accountability for cach participant's portion of
contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for future claims. Should
any participant's premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs, and losses, the
remaining participants’ portion of Health Plan assets can be used to satisfy the payments
allocated to that participant. In the event of Health Plan termination, any assets
remaining in the Health Plan in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and
losses will ultimately be returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares. In
the opinion of the Home Office, the Health Plan has sufficient assets to meet a
significant portion of current and estimated future costs, losses and future claims;
accordingly, the Center's expense for the year ended December 31, 2018, totaled

Defined contribution plan

Effective November 1, 1996, the Home Office established a defined contribution plan,
Health Concepts, Ltd. 401(k) Plan, for the benefit of the employees of the Home
Office, its participating nursing facilities, and a business owned by the Center's
shareholders. The plan covers all employees who meet the eligibility requirements,
which include attainment of age 18 and the completion of more than 999 hours of
service in a prior year. The Home Office, the Center and ten nursing facilities owned by
the Center’s shareholders participate in the plan.

For 2018, the plan provides that the Center will match 75% of employee contributions
up to a maximum match of 7.5% of eligible compensation. The Center’s contributions
to the plan totaled $174,075 for the year ended December 31, 2018.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS AND
CONTINGENCIES

Medicaid eligibility determination delays

Since early 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Center has determined should be
eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has
been filed with the State. The Center provides services to these patients and recognizes
related revenue during the period in which the State has not made a determination
related to a completed application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending
Application”). Amounts reported as patient services receivables related to Medicaid
Pending Applications that have been pending for less than 90 days and those that have
been pending for 90 days or more for which the Center has not requested an advance
payment (see Note 1) may be subject to subsequent denial by the State at some future
date. Management believes that the State will ultimately determine that patients for
whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are eligible for Medicaid and that any
potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently denied by the State
will not have a material adverse effect on the Center’s financial position.

Contingency

In a prior year, the Center was a party to a scttlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Center paid
an agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement
agreement, the Center became a party to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with
the OIG. The CIA requires that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance
Program that promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled
nursing facilities affiliated with or owned, operated or managed by the Home Office,
including the Center. The CIA is for a five-year period commencing September 2016.
During the year ended December 31, 2017, the OIG accepted the Annual Report
submitted by the Home Office pursuant to the CIA. The Home Office is compliant
with the requirements of the CIA as of December 31, 2018.

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT
ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Description of business

Ryan Health Center, Inc. (the "Center") d/b/a Morgan Health Center, owns and
operates a 120-bed nursing facility located in Johnston, Rhode Island.

The Center provides services to patients, principally from Rhode Island, with third-
party financial coverage (principally Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients
who are responsible for their own financial obligations.

Recently adopted accounting pronouncements

Revenue recognition

In May 2014, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) issued Accounting
Standards Update (“ASU”) no. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (“Topic
606”), with several clarifying updates issued subsequently. In conjunction with Topic
606, a new subtopic, Accounting Standards Codification ("ASC") 340-40, Other Assets
and Deferred Costs — Contracts mith Customers, was also issued. ‘The updated standard
replaces most existing revenue recognition and certain cost guidance under accounting
principles generally accepted in the United States of America ("U.S. GAAP").
Collectively, we refer to Topic 606 and Subtopic 340-40 as “ASC 606”. ASC 606
amends existing accounting standards for revenue recognition and establishes principles
for recognizing revenue upon the transfer of promised goods or services to customers
based on the expected consideration to be received in exchange for those goods and
services. The Center adopted ASC 606 effective January 1, 2019 using the modified
retrospective transition method. The Center has determined that the adjustments using
the modified retrospective approach did not have a material impact on the date of the

initial application. The Center did not apply any practical expedients in implementing
ASC 606.

Use of estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP requires
management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of
assets and liabilities, and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the
financial statements, and the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the
reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates. The allowance for
doubtful accounts is a significant estimate used in the preparation of the accompanying
financial statements.

Cash and cash equivalents

The Center considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three
months or less to be cash equivalents. At December 31, 2019, the Center had no cash
equivalents.

===== PAGE 1260 =====
[OCR]
NOTE 1.

RYAN HEALTH CENTER, INC.
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
DECEMBER 31, 2019

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS AND SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT
ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Cash and cash equivalents (continued

‘The Center maintains cash balances at various financial institutions in accounts insured
by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation ("FDIC"). The Center monitors its
concentration of deposits by obtaining and evaluating bank ratings on a quarterly basis.
At December 31, 2019, the Center had $887,214 of deposits in excess of the FDIC-
insured limits.

Patient services receivables

Patient services receivables are stated at the amount the Center expects to collect.

Under Rhode Island General Law Title 40, Chapter 8, Section 6.1(b)(2) , Haman Services,
Medical Assistance, Provider Care During Pendeney of Application, Uncompensated Care While
Determination is Overdue, wpon the Center’s request, the State of Rhode Island (the
"State") is required to make payments to the Center for charges related to a patient that
the Center has determined should be eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed
application for Medicaid benefits filed with the State has been pending for 90 days ot
more ("advance payments"); such advance payments may not be recovered, offset or
recouped by the State upon a subsequent determination by the State that the patient is
not cligible for Medicaid. Consequently, advance payments received by the Center prior
to the date the State has made a determination related to the patient’s cligibility for
Medicaid are offset against the patient services receivables included in the accompanying
balance sheet. Advance payments received by the Center related to Medicaid claims
subsequently approved and paid by the State are required to be repaid to the State
through an ongoing reconciliation process and, consequently, are reported within
current liabilities, third-party advances in the accompanying balance sheet. At
December 31, 2019, advance payments offset against patient services receivables totaled
$156,177.

The Center provides for probable uncollectible amounts through a charge to provision
for losses and a credit to the allowance for doubtful accounts based on its assessment of
the current status of individual accounts. Balances that are still outstanding after the
Center has used reasonable collection efforts are written off through a charge to the
allowance for doubtful accounts and a credit to receivables. The Center does not obtain
collateral for amounts due.

Approximately 16% and 5% of the Center’s patient services receivables is due from the
Rhode Island Medicaid and federal Medicare programs, respectively.

At December 31, 2019 and 2018, patient services receivables was $1,424,772 and
$831,136, respectively.

Fixed assets

Fixed assets are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is provided
using the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets, ranging from
4 years to 40 years. Depreciation expense totaled $84,926 for the year ended
December 31, 2019.

Fixed assets (continued

The Center evaluates long-lived assets held and used by the Center for impairment
whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the
asset may not be recoverable. An impairment loss is recognized if the sum of the
expected undiscounted future cash flows from the use and disposition of the asset is
less than its carrying amount. Generally, the amount of impairment loss is measured as
the difference between the carrying amount of the asset and the estimated fair value of
the asset. The Center did not record an impairment loss during the year ended
December 31, 2019.

Debt issuance costs

Debt issuance costs are being amortized over the term of the related debt using the
straight-line method, which approximates the effective interest method.

Income taxes

The Center has elected to be taxed as an S Corporation under the Internal Revenue
Code. Accordingly, the shareholders include the income or loss of the Center on their
respective income tax returns, In accordance with ASC 740, Income Taxes, the Center
applies the “more likely than not” threshold to the recognition and derecognition of tax
positions for its financial statements. Management has evaluated the Center’s tax
positions and has concluded that there were no uncertain tax positions that qualified for
either recognition or disclosure in these financial statements.

Revenue recognition

The Center adopted Topic 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, on January 1, 2019.
Revenue is measured based on consideration specified in a contract with a customer,
and excludes any amounts collected on behalf of third parties. ‘The Center recognizes
revenue when it satisfies a petformance obligation by transferring control over a
product or service to a customer. The majority of the Center’s revenue originates from
contracts with customers to provide various healthcare services. The majority of the
Centet’s services represent a bundle of services that are not capable of being distinct
and as such, are treated as a single performance obligation that is satisfied over time as
the services are rendered. The Center’s standard payment terms are within 30 days from
billing.

The Center determines the transaction price based on contractually agreed upon rates,
adjusted for estimates of variable consideration, such as implicit price concessions.
Variable consideration also exists as the Center's third-party revenue is paid principally
at prospectively determined rates. Retroactive adjustments are considered in the
recognition of revenue on an estimated basis in the period the related services are
rendered such that net patient service revenues are only recorded to the extent that it is
probable that a significant reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognized will
not occur in the future. Any differences between the estimated amounts accrued, and
interim and final settlements are adjusted in future periods as adjustments become
known or as years are no longer subject to such audits, reviews and investigations.

Disageregation of revenues

The Center operates as a skilled nursing facility and provides services to patients,
ptincipally from Rhode Island, who have third-party financial coverage (principally
Rhode Island Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are responsible
for their own financial obligations. Therefore, the Center’s viability is dependent on a
number of factors such as licensed bed capacity, occupancy rates, mix of patient by
payer and case type, the rates of reimbursement, changes to Medicaid and Medicare
programs, and the Center’s ability to collect on its contracts. All of the Center’s net
patient service revenue for financial reporting purposes are recorded over time as the
services are rendered.

Net patient service revenue from third-party payers totaled $9,108,134 for the year
ended December 31, 2019. Net patient service revenue from private payers totaled
$1,241,412 for the year ended December 31, 2019.

Significant risks and uncertainties

Laws and regulations governing Medicare, Medicaid and other governmental
reimbursement programs are extremely complex and subject to interpretation. As a
result, there is at least a reasonable possibility that recorded estimates could change by a
material amount in the near term, It is management’s opinion that the Center is in
compliance with applicable laws and regulations; however, the possibility of government
teview and interpretation exists. Compliance with such laws and regulations can be
subject to future government review and interpretation, as well as significant regulatory
action; failure to comply with such laws and regulations can result in fines, penalties and
exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid programs.

Third-party advances
The Center records advances from third-party payors as a liability upon reccipt.
Self-insurance costs

It is the Center’s policy to fund workers’ compensation and health care self-insurance
costs accrued. ‘I'he provision for such costs includes estimates of the ultimate costs for
both reported claims and claims incurred but not reported.

Subsequent events

The Center has evaluated subsequent events through April 15, 2020, the date that the
accompanying financial statements were available to be issued. Except as disclosed in
Note 5, there were no material events that required recognition or additional disclosure.

Management fee

The Center has a management agreement with Health Concepts, Ltd. (the "Home

services, principally management services. The agreement expires in May 2032, unless
automatically renewed for an additional 15-year term in December 2031. The

Center's shareholders participate in the Plan and have transferred their workers!
compensation insurance to the Plan.

Workers' compensation insurance (continued)

The Plan provides for the payment of administration, claims and tisk management
costs, as well as payment for losses. Lach participant makes monthly contributions
(premium payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workers’ Compensation
Trust (the "T'rust") through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to
establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The reserve is held in trust and invested
by the Plan trustee. The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a
commetcial insurance carrier to protect the Trust's assets from individual losses in
excess of $450,000. In addition, the Trust carries a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode
Island Department of Labor, collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a
bank, for which no amounts are outstanding at December 31, 2019.

The Trust Committee (the "Committee") maintains separate accountability for each
participant’s portion of contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for
future claims. Should any participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims,
costs, and losses, the remaining participants’ portion of Trust assets can be used to
satisfy the payments allocated to that participant. In the event of Plan termination, any
assets remaining in the Trust in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and
losses will ultimately be returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares.

In the opinion of the Committee, the Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant
portion of current and estimated future costs, losses and future claims; accordingly, the
Center's required premium for the year ended December 31, 2019, totaled $170,873, an
amount that, in management's opinion, is below the premium it would pay to a
commercial insurance carrier if the Plan did not exist and did not achieve significant
savings as a result of the loss control program and monitoring services provided by the
Home Office.

The Plan's net assets at December 31, 2019, include cash and investments with a cost,
which approximates fair value, of $758,400 (unaudited).

Health insurance

Effective January 1, 2018, the Home Office established a self-insured health insurance
plan (the "Health Plan"). ‘The Home Office, the Center and other nursing facilities and
a business owned by the Center's shareholders participate in the Health Plan and have
transferred their health insurance to the Health Plan. The Health Pian provides for the
payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as well as payment for
losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium payments), as required,
to the Health Plan account maintained at the Home Office to pay current costs and
losses and to establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The Health Plan carries
excess loss insurance coverage with a commercial insurance carrier to protect the Health
Plan's assets from individual losses in excess of $100,000.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS AND
CONTINGENCIES

Medicaid eligibility determination delays

Since early 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Center has determined should be
eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has
been filed with the State. The Center provides services to these patients and recognizes
related revenue during the period in which the State has not made a determination
related to a completed application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending
Application”). Amounts reported as patient services receivables related to Medicaid
Pending Applications that have been pending for less than 90 days and those that have
been pending for 90 days or more for which the Center has not requested an advance
payment (see Note 1) may be subject to subsequent denial by the State at some future
date. Management believes that the State will ultimately determine that patients for
whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are eligible for Medicaid and that any
potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently denied by the State
will not have a material adverse effect on the Centet’s financial position.

Contingency

In a prior year, the Center was a party to a settlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Center paid
an agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement
agreement, the Center became a party to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with
the OIG. The CIA requires that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance
Program that promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled
nursing facilities affiliated with or owned, operated or managed by the Home Office,
including the Center. The CIA is for a five-year period commencing September 2016.
During the years ended December 31, 2017 and 2018, and in January 2020, the OIG
accepted the Annual Reports submitted by the Home Office pursuant to the CIA. The
Home Office is compliant with the requirements of the CIA as of December 31, 2019,

Continuing operations

The Center has a shareholders’ deficiency and a working capital ratio of less than 1.0 at
December 31, 2019. ‘These conditions are significant to the Center's ability to continue
operations and to meet its obligations. The Center has evaluated these conditions and
agreed with the Home Office to delay payment of accrued management fees owed to
the Home Office and to provide other support, as needed, allowing the Center the
ability to continue to operate and to meet its current obligations. These factors mitigate
doubt about the Center's ability to continue as a going concern.

UNCERTAINTY

In 2020, the World Health Organization has declared COVID-19 to constitute a "Public
Health Emergency of International Concern." Disruptions to the Center's business
Operations could occur as a result from the supply and quarantine of employees,
residents, and vendors. Given the uncertainty of this situation, an estimate of the
financial impact to the Center, if any, cannot be reasonably estimated at this time.

not eligible for Medicaid. Consequently, advance payments received by the Center prior
to the date the State has made a determination related to the patient’s eligibility for
Medicaid are offset against the patient services receivables included in the accompanying
balance sheet.

Rhode Island Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are responsible
for théir own financial obligations. Therefore, the Center’s viability is dependent on a
nufhber of factors such as licensed bed capacity, occupancy rates, mix of patient by

<Spayer and case type, the rates of reimbursement, changes to Medicaid and Medicare

programs, and the Center’s ability to collect on its contracts. All of the Center’s net
patient service revenue for financial reporting purposes are recorded over time as the
services are rendered.

Net patient service revenue from third-party payers totaled $8,520,295 for the year
ended December 31, 2020. Net patient service revenue from private payers totaled
$697,379 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

Significant risks and uncertainties

Laws and regulations governing Medicare, Medicaid and other governmental
reimbursement programs are extremely complex and subject to interpretation. As a
result, there is at least a reasonable possibility that recorded estimates could change by a
material amount in the near term. It is management’s opinion that the Center is in
compliance with applicable laws and regulations; however, the possibility of government
review and interpretation exists. Compliance with such laws and regulations can be
subject to future government review and interpretation, as well as significant regulatory
action; failure to comply with such laws and regulations can result in fines, penalties and
exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid programs.

OTHER LOAN ‘AND NOTES PAYABLE AND SUBSEQUENT EVENT

On April 20,°2020, the Center received a loan in the amount of $1,254,200 under the
Paycheck*Protection Program ("PPP") with its bank as part of the Small Business Act
(“SBA”). The PPP, which was established as part of the CARES Act, provides for loans
to’qualifying businesses for amounts up to 2.5 times certain average monthly payroll

‘expenses of the qualifying business. ‘The loans and accrued interest, or a portion thereof,

may be forgiven after qwenty-four weeks so long as the borrower uses the loan proceeds
for eligible purposes, including payroll, benefits, rent, mortgage interest, and utilities,
and maintains its payroll levels. Not more than 40% of the amount forgiven can be
attributable to non-payroll costs. The PPP loan will be deferred until the SBA remits the
loan forgiveness, if applicable, to the lender.

The Center currently intends to use the proceeds for purposes consistent with the PPP,
however, there can be no assurances that the Center will ultimately meet the conditions
for forgiveness of the loan or that the Center will not take actions that could cause the
Center to be ineligible for forgiveness of the loan, in whole or in part.

OTHER LOAN AND NOTES PAYABLE AND SUBSEQUENT EVENT
CONTINUED

U.S. GAAP does not contain authoritative accounting standards for forgivable loans
provided by governmental entities to a for profit entity. Absent authoritative accounting
standards, interpretative guidance issued and commonly applied by financial statement
preparers allow for the selection of accounting policies amongst acceptable alternatives.

Based on the facts and circumstances, the Center has determined it most appropriate to
account for the PPP loan proceeds under the debt model. The Center deemed the debt
model to be the most appropriate accounting policy for this arrangement as the
underlying PPP loan is a legal form of debt and there are significant contingencies
outside of the control of the Center, mainly related to the third-party approval process
for forgiveness. Under the debt model, the Center recognizes the proceeds received as
debt, recognizes periodic interest expense in the period in which the interest accrues at
the stated interest rate and defers recognition of any pogéntial forgiveness of the loan
principal or interest until the period in which the Cente# has been legally released for its
obligation by the lender. Accrued interest and_,principal payments on the loan will
commence, at a maximum, 10 months after the*end of the 24-week covered period if
the loan has not been forgiven in full. The Joan matures two years from the date of first
disbursement of proceeds to the Home,*“If the loan if not forgiven, the note accrues
interest from the date of disbursemene at 1%,

As of the date of this report, the.PPP loan forgiveness has not been finalized. There can
be no assurance given that the"Home will obtain forgiveness of the PPP Loan in whole
or in part. In order to agply for the PPP Loan, the Center certified that, among other
things, the current egénomic uncertainty made the PPP Loan request necessary to
support its ongoing operations. In addition, PPP loans under the CARES Act may be
subject to cerwiln rules, regulations and procedures applicable to the SBA Loan
Program, which includes PPP loans under the CARES Act. The interpretation and
applicability of these rules, regulations and procedures is unclear, as some of them have
not béen referenced in the CARES Act itself ot in the guidance and interpretations
issued by the SBA to date.

“Tf it is determined that the Center was not eligible to receive the PPP Loan, or that the

Center has not adequately complied with the rules, regulations and procedures
applicable to the SBA’s Loan Program, the Center could be subject to penalties and
could be required to repay the PPP Loan in its entirety.

UNEARNED CARES ACT FUNDS AND SUBSEQUENT EVENT

During the year ended December 31, 2020, the Center received Provider Relief Fund
PRP”) and Coronavirus Relief Fund (“CRE”) distributions in the approximate
amounts of $834,000 and $255,000, respectively, provided for under the CARES Act
from the U.S. Department and Health and Human Services ("HHS") and_ the
Department of the Treasury. The distributions from the PRF and CRE are not subject
to repayment provided the Center is able to attest to and comply with the terms and
conditions of the funding, including demonstrating that the funds received have been
used for healthcare-related expenses or “lost revenues” (as defined by HHS) attributable
to COVID-19.

sinpensation insurance

Effegtive January 1, 1994, the Home Office received permission from the Rhode Island
Department of Tso to establish a pooled self-insured workers' compensation plan (the

Plan"). The Home Office, the Center and cight nursing facilities owned by the
Center's shareholders participate in the Plan and have transferred their workers!
compensation insurance to the Plan.

The Plan provides for the payment of administration, claims and risk management
costs, as well as payment for losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions
(premium payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workers’ Compensation
Trust (the Trust") through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to
establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The reserve is held in trust and invested
by the Plan trustee. ‘The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a
commercial insurance cartier to protect the Trust's assets from individual losses in
excess of $450,000. In addition, the Trust carties a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode
Island Department of Labor, collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a
bank, for which no amounts are outstanding at December 31, 2020.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS AND

CONTINGENCIES
Medicaid eligibility determination delays

O'Since early 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Center has determined should be
cligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has
been filed with the State. The Center provides services to these patients and recognizes
related revenue during the period in which the State has not made a determination
related to a completed application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending
Application”). Amounts reported as patient services receivables related to Medicaid
Pending Applications that have been pending for less than 90 days and those that have
been pending for 90 days or more for which the Center has not requested an advance
payment (see Note 1) may be subject to subsequent denial by the State at some future
date. Management believes that the State will ultimately determine that patients for
whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are cligible for Medicaid and that any
potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently denied by the State
will not have a material adverse effect on the Center’s financial position.

Contingency

In a prior year, the Center was a party to a settlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Center paid
an agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement
agreement, the Center became a party to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with
the OIG. The CIA requires that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance
Program that promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled
nursing facilities affiliated with or owned, operated or managed .by the Home Office,
including the Center. The CIA is for a five-year period commencing September 2016.
During the years ended December 31, 2017 and 2018, andvin January 2020 and January
2021, the OIG accepted the Annual Reports submitted by the Home Office pursuant to
the CLA. The Home Office is compliant with the* requirements of the CIA as of
December 31, 2020. a

Continuing operations

‘The Center has a shareholders! deficierity and a working capital ratio of less than 1.0 at
December 31, 2020. These conditisns are significant to the Center's ability to continue
operations and to meet its obligations. The Center has evaluated these conditions and
agreed with the Home Office to delay payment of accrued management fees owed to
the Home Office and té* provide other support, as needed, allowing the Center the
ability to continue to-6perate and to meet its current obligations. This factor, along with
PPP and CARES$*Act funding received, mitigates doubt about the Center's ability to
continue as a going concern,

UNCERTAINTY DUE TO COVID-19
In March 2020, the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak to

Constitute a “Public Health Emergency of International Concern.” Disruptions to the
~ Center’s business operations occurred during 2020 and continue into 2021 as a result

from the supply and quarantine of employees, residents, and vendors. The Center,
along with most skilled nursing facilities throughout the U.S., has experienced a
significant decline in admissions and census and additional costs associated with
tetaining and attracting staff and protective medical supplies due to the COVID-19
pandemic, Given the uncertainty of the situation, an estimate of the financial impact to
the Center, if any, cannot be reasonably estimated at this time.

Report on the Financial Statements

We have audited the accompanying financial statements of Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the “Home’”),
Project No. 016-43122, which comprise the balance sheet as of December 31, 2018, and the related
statements of operations, shareholders’ deficiency, and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related
notes to the financial statements.

Management’s Responsibility for the Financial Statements

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these financial statements in
accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America; this includes the
design, implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and _ fair
presentation of financial statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.

Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit. We conducted
our audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America and the
standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards, issued by the Comptroller
General of the United States. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain
reasonable assurance about whether the financial statements are free from material misstatement.

An audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the amounts and disclosures in the
financial statements. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment, including the assessment of
the tisks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether duc to fraud or error. In making
those risk assessments, the auditor considers internal control relevant to the entity’s preparation and fair
presentation of the financial statements in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the
circumstances, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the entity’s internal
control. Accordingly, we express no such opinion. An audit also includes evaluating the appropriateness of
accounting policies used and the reasonableness of significant accounting estimates made by management,
as well as evaluating the overall presentation of the financial statements.

We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our
audit opinion.

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS

Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the “Home’”) d/b/a Riverview Healthcare Community, owns
and operates a 190-bed nursing facility located in Coventry, Rhode Island. The Home
provides services to patients, principally from Rhode Island, with third-party financial
coverage (principally Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are
responsible for their own financial obligations.

The Home is regulated by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
(“HUD”) as to operating methods under Section 232 of the National Housing Act of 1959
(the “Act”). The Section 232 Housing Program was formed under the Act and provides
HUD-insured mortgage notes to participating developments (see Note 4).

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Recently issued but not yet effective accounting pronouncements

Revenue recognition

In May 2014, the Financial Accounting Standards Boatd (“FASB”) issued Accounting
Standards Update (“ASU”) No. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts nith Customers (Accounting
Standards Codification ("ASC") Topic 606), as amended (commonly referred to as "ASC
606"), which requires an entity to recognize revenue to depict the transfer of promised
goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration which the entity
expects to be entitled to receive in exchange for those goods or services. ASC 606 replaces
most existing revenue recognition standards in accounting principles generally accepted in
the United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”), including industry-specific standards, when it
becomes effective. For annual reporting periods, this standard is effective for the Home on
January 1, 2019, and for interim periods within annual periods that begin one year later.
The standard permits the use of cither the retrospective or cumulative-effect transition
method. The Home is currently compicting its initial assessment and evaluation of the
impact that ASC 606 will have on the Home’s financial statements and related disclosures.

The Home expects to retrospectively adopt ASC 606 effective January 1, 2019. As a result,
substantially all amounts previously reported as provision for losses on patient services
receivables will now be considered an implicit price concession and will be recognized as a
reduction of net patient service revenue. The adoption of ASC 606 will also result in
expanded disclosures that will enable the users of the financial statements to better
understand the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty, if any, of revenues and cash flows
arising from contracts with customers.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Recently issued but not yet effective accounting pronouncements (continued)

Statement of cash flons

In November 2016, the FASB issued ASU No. 2016-18, Statement of Cash Flows (Topic 230):
Restricted Cash (a consensus of the Emerging Issues Task Force) (“ASU 2016-18”), which requires an
entity to present restricted cash and cash equivalents together with unrestricted cash and
cash equivalents in the statement of cash flows. Under ASU 2016-18, an entity will be
required to disclose in the financial statements how the statement of cash flows reconciles to
the balance sheet, if restricted cash and cash equivalents are presented separate from
unrestricted cash and cash equivalents on the balance sheet, and the nature of the restrictions
at the balance sheet date. This new guidance is effective for years beginning after
December 15, 2018, with early adoption permitted. Upon adoption of the amendments in
ASU 2016-18, the Home will present within the statement of cash flows the change during
the period in total cash and cash equivalents, including amounts generally desctibed as
restricted cash and cash equivalents, The amendments will be applied retrospectively.

Use of estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP requires
management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets
and liabilities, and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial
statements. Estimates also affect the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the
reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates. The allowance for
doubtful accounts is a significant estimate used in the preparation of the accompanying
financial statements.

Cash and cash equivalents, escrow deposits and replacement reserve

The Home considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or
less to be cash equivalents. At December 31, 2018, the Home had no cash equivalents.

The Home maintains cash balances at various financial institutions in accounts insured by
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”), At December 31, 2018, these
balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $1,850,882.

The mortgagee holds the mortgage escrow deposits (noninterest-bearing) and the
replacement reserve (interest-bearing) in FDIC-insured accounts. At December 31, 2018,

these balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $413,035.

The Home monitors its concentration of deposits, including those held by the mortgagee, by
obtaining and evaluating bank ratings on a quarterly basis.

Receivables

Tenant accounts receivable and Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance receivable are stated at
the amount the Home expects to collect.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Receivables (continued)

Under Rhode Island General Law Title 40, Chapter 8, Section 6.1(b)(2) , Human Services,
Medical Assistance, Provider Care During Pendency of Application, Uncompensated Care While
Determination is Overdue, upon the Home’s request, the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) is
required to make payments to the Home for charges related to a patient that the Home has
determined should be eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for
Medicaid benefits filed with the State has been pending for 90 days or more (“advance
payments”); such advance payments may not be recovered, offset or recouped by the State
upon a subsequent determination by the State that the patient is not eligible for Medicaid.
Consequently, advance payments received by the Home prior to the date the State has made
a determination related to the patient’s eligibility for Medicaid are offset against the tenant
accounts receivable included in the accompanying balance sheet. Advance payments reccived
by the Home related to Medicaid claims subsequently approved and paid by the State are
required to be repaid to the State through an ongoing reconciliation process and,
consequently, are reported within current liabilities, third-party advances in the
accompanying balance sheet. At December 31, 2018, advance payments offset against tenant
receivables totaled $1,397,970.

The Home provides for probable uncollectible amounts through a charge to provision for
losses and a credit to the allowance for doubtful accounts based on its assessment of the
current status of individual accounts. Balances that are still outstanding after the Home has
used reasonable collection efforts are written off through a charge to the allowance for
doubtful accounts and a credit to receivables. The Home does not obtain collateral for
amounts due.

Approximately 13% and 5% of the Home’s tenant accounts receivable and
Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance receivable is due from the Rhode Island Medicaid and
federal Medicare programs, respectively.

Fixed assets

Fixed assets are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is provided
using the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets, ranging from 4
years to 40 years. Depreciation expense totaled $350,264 for the year ended December 31,
2018.

The Home evaluates long-lived asscts held and used by the Home for impaitment whenever
events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the asset may not be
recoverable. An impairment loss is recognized if the sum of the expected undiscounted
future cash flows from the use and disposition of the asset is less than its carrying amount.
Generally, the amount of impaitment loss is measured as the difference between the carrying
amount of the asset and the estimated fair value of the asset. The Home did not record an
impairment loss during the year ended December 31, 2018.

Income taxes

The Home has elected to be taxed as an S Corporation under the Internal Revenue
Code. Accordingly, the shareholders include the income or loss of the Home on their
respective income tax returns. In accordance with ASC 740, Income Taxes, the Home applies
the “more likely than not” threshold to the recognition and derecognition of tax positions
for its financial statements. Management has evaluated the Home’s tax positions and has
concluded that there were no uncertain tax positions that qualified for either recognition or
disclosure in these financial statements.

Net patient service revenue

Net patient service revenue is reported at estimated net amounts realizable from residents,
third-party payors (principally “Medicare and Rhode Island Medicaid”) and others for
services rendered.

The Home’s third-party revenue is paid principally at prospectively determined rates.
Retroactive adjustments are considered in the recognition of revenue on an estimated basis
in the petiod the telated services are tendered; any differences between the estimated
amounts accrued, and interim and final settlements are adjusted in future periods as
adjustments become known or as years are no longer subject to such audits, reviews and
investigations.

RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS

Management fee

The Home has a management agreement with Health Concepts, Ltd. (the “Home Office”), a
company owned by the shareholders, to provide home office services, principally
management services. The agreement expires in May 2032, unless automatically renewed for
an additional 15-year term in December 2031. The HUD-approved management fee is a
maximum of 7% of net patient service revenue. In 2018, management fees totaled 6% of net
patient service revenue, and amounted to $1,007,445 for the year ended December 31, 2018.

Workers’ compensation insurance

Effective January 1, 1994, the Home Office received permission from the Rhode Island
Department of Labor to establish a pooled self-insured workers’ compensation plan (the
“Plan”), The Home Office, the Home and eight nursing facilities owned by the Home’s
shareholders participate in the Plan and have transferred their workers’ compensation
insurance to the Plan.

The Plan provides for the payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as
well as payment for losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium
payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workers’ Compensation Trust (the
“Trust”) through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to establish a
cumulative reserve for future claims. The reserve is held in trust and invested by the Plan
trustee. The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a commercial insurance
carrier to protect the Trust’s assets from individual losses in excess of $450,000. In addition,
the T'rust carries a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode Island Department of Labor,
collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a bank, for which no amounts are
outstanding at December 31, 2018.

The Trust Committee (the “Committee”) maintains separate accountability for each
participant’s portion of contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for
future claims. Should any patticipant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs
and losses, the remaining participants’ portion of the Trust assets can be used to satisfy the
payments allocated to that participant. In the event of Plan termination, any assets
remaining in the Trust in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will
ultimately be returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares.

In the opinion of the Committee, the Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion
of current and estimated future costs, losses and future claims; accordingly, the Home’s
required premium for the year ended December 31, 2018, totaled $263,937, an amount that,
in management’s opinion, is below the premium it would pay to a commercial insurance
carrier if the Plan did not exist and did not achieve significant savings as a result of the loss
control program and monitoring services provided by the Home Office.

Defined contribution plan

Effective November 1, 1996, the Home Office established a defined contribution plan,

For 2018, the plan provides that the Home will match 75% of employee contributions up to
a maximum match of 7.5% of eligible compensation. ‘The Home’s contributions to the plan
totaled $215,657 for the year ended December 31, 2018.

Health insurance

Effective January 1, 2018, the Home Office established a self-insured health insurance plan
(the “Health Plan”). The Home Office, the Home and other nursing facilities and a
business owned by the Home’s shareholders participate in the Health Plan and have
transferred their health insurance to the Health Plan. The Health Plan provides for the
payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as well as payment for losses.
Fach participant makes monthly contributions (premium payments), as required, to the
Health Plan account maintained at the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to
establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The Health Plan carrics excess loss
insurance coverage with a commercial insurance carrier to protect the Health Plan’s assets
from individual losses in excess of $100,000.

The Home Office maintains separate accountability for each participant’s portion of
contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for future claims. Should any
patticipant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs, and losses, the remaining
participants’ portion of Health Plan assets can be used to satisfy the payments allocated to
that participant. In the event of Health Plan termination, any assets remaining in the Health
Plan in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will ultimately be retarned
to the participants based on their pro rata shares. In the opinion of the Home Office, the
Health Pian has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion of current and estimated future
costs, losses and future claims; the Home’s expense for the year ended December 31, 2018,
totaled $792,438.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS, COMMITMENT
AND CONTINGENCIES

Medicaid eligibility determination delays

Since carly 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Home has determined should be eligible for
Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has been filed with
the State. The Home provides services to these patients and recognizes related revenue
during the period in which the State has not made a determination related to a completed
application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending Application”). Amounts reported as
tenant accounts receivable related to Medicaid Pending Applications that have been pending
for less than 90 days and those that have been pending for 90 days or more for which the
Home has not requested an advance payment (see Note 2) may be subject to subsequent
denial by the State at some future date. Management believes that the State will ultimately
determine that patients for whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are cligible for
Medicaid and that any potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently
denied by the State will not have a material adverse effect on the Home’s financial position.

Commitment

In a prior year, the Home was a party to a settlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Home paid an
agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement
agreement, the Home became a patty to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with the
OIG. ‘The CIA requires that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance
Program that promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled
nursing facilities affiliated with or owned, operated or managed by the Home Office,
including the Home. The CIA is for a five-year period commencing September 2016.
During the year ended December 31, 2017, the OIG accepted the Annual Report submitted
by the Home Office pursuant to the CIA. The Home Office is compliant with the
requirements of the CIA as of December 31, 2018.

Continuing operations

The Home incurred a net loss in 2018, has incurred net losses in the past two years, has a
shareholders’ deficiency and a working capital ratio of less than 1.0. These conditions are
significant to the Home’s ability to continue operations and to meet its obligations. ‘The
Home has evaluated these conditions and agreed with the Home Office to delay payment of
accrued management fees owed to the Home Office, as needed, allowing the Home the
ability to continue to operate and to meet its current obligations. This factor mitigates doubt
about the Home’s ability to continue as a going concern.

INDEPENDENT AUDITOR’S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL

GOVERNMENT AUDITING STANDARDS

To the Shareholders
Riverview Nursing Home Inc.
Coventry, Rhode Isiand

We have audited, in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America
and the standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards issued by the
Comptroller General of the United States, the financial statements of Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the
“Home”), which comprise the balance sheet as of December 31, 2018, and the related statements of
operations, shareholders’ deficiency and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related notes to the
financial statements, and have issued our report thereon dated March 29, 2019.

Internal Control over Financial Reporting

In planning and performing our audit of the financial statements, we considered the Home’s internal control
over financial reporting (internal control) to determine the audit procedures that are appropriate in the
circumstances for the purpose of expressing our opinion on the financial statements, but not for the
purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal control. Accordingly, we do
not express an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal control.

A. deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or
employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct,
misstatements on a timely basis. A material weakness is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in
internal control, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the entity’s
financial statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected on a timely basis. A significant deficiency
is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in internal control that is less severe than a material
weakness, yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance.

Our consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described in the first paragraph of this
section and was not designed to identify all deficiencies in internal control that might be material weaknesses
or significant deficiencies. Given these limitations, during our audit we did not identify any deficiencies in
internal control that we consider to be matetial weaknesses. However, material weaknesses may exist that
have not been identified.

audit findings:

Finding 1 - The audit report issued on April 21, 2017, by HUD O1G, numbered 2017-BO-1005,
disclosed a finding that service charges at five FHA-insured nursing homes did not always comply with
management agreements, duc to inconsistencies between the management agreements and the HUD
Management Certifications. ‘The finding stated the management agent, Heaith Concepts, charged the
nursing homes’ owners separately for services that should have been included and paid for as part of the
management agreement.

Status - In June 2017, Health Concepts revised the management agreement to clarify what costs may be
charged to the nursing homes. In December 2017, HUD requested and Health Concepts agreed to an
agreed-upon procedures engagement related to identifying any payments made by the Home for services
outside of the management agreement. The engagement did not identify any material payments for such
services, In late 2018, OIG reported that it did not accept the audit results. The management agent
returned funds to the facilities, to bring resolution to the finding, and was notified on March 5, 2019,
that OIG had accepted the resolution.

Report on the Financial Statements

We have audited the accompanying financial statements of Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the “Home”), Project
No. 016-43122, which comprise the balance sheet as of December 31, 2019, and the related statements of
operations, shareholders’ deficiency, and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related notes to the financial
statements.

Management’s Responsibility for the Financial Statements

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these financial statements in accordance
with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America; this includes the design,
implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and fait presentation of financial
statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.

Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit. We conducted our
audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America and the standards
applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards, issued by the Comptroller General of the
United States. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements ate free from material misstatement.

An audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the amounts and disclosures in the
financial statements. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment, including the assessment of the
tisks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud or error. In making those risk
assessments, the auditor considers internal control relevant to the entity’s preparation and fair presentation of the
financial statements in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the
purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the entity’s internal control. Accordingly, we express no
such opinion. An audit also includes evaluating the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the
reasonableness of significant accounting estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall
presentation of the financial statements.

We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit
opinion.

Opinion

In our opinion, the financial statements referred to above present fairly, in all material respects, the financial
position of Riverview Nursing Home Inc., as of December 31, 2019, and the results of its operations and its cash

flows for the year then ended in accordance with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of
America.

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS

Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the “Home”) d/b/a Riverview Healthcare Community, owns
and operates a 190-bed nursing facility located in Coventry, Rhode Island. The Home
provides services to patients, principally from Rhode Island, with third-party financial
coverage (ptincipally Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are
responsible for their own financial obligations.

The Home is regulated by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
(“HUD”) as to operating methods under Section 232 of the National Housing Act of 1959
(the “Act”). ‘The Section 232 Housing Program was formed under the Act and provides
HUD-insured mortgage notes to participating developments (see Note 4).

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Recently adopted accounting pronouncements

Revenue recognition

In May 2014, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) issued Accounting
Standards Update (“ASU”) No. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (“Topic 606”),
with several clarifying updates issued subsequently. In conjunction with Topic 606, a new
subtopic, Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) 340-40, Other Assets and Deferred Costs —
Contracts with Customers, was also issued. The updated standard replaces most existing revenue
recognition and certain cost guidance under accounting principles generally accepted in the
United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”). Collectively, we refer to Topic 606 and Subtopic
340-40 as “ASC 606”. ASC 606 amends existing accounting standards for revenue
recognition and establishes principles for recognizing revenue upon the transfer of promised
goods or services to customers based on the expected consideration to be received in
exchange for those goods and services. The Home adopted ASC 606 effective January 1,
2019 using the modified retrospective transition method. The Home has determined that the
adjustments using the modified retrospective approach did not have a material impact on the
date of the initial application. The Home did not apply any practical expedients in
implementing ASC 606.

Restricted cash

In November 2016, FASB issued ASU No. 2016-18, Statement of Cash Flows (Topic 230):
Restricted Cash (“ASU 2016-18”), which required that restricted cash and restricted cash
equivalents be included with cash and cash equivalents when reconciling the
beginning-of-period and end-of-period total amounts shown on the statement of cash flows.
ASU 2016-18 was effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2018 and
interim periods within fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2019.

Use of estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP requires
management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets
and liabilities, and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial
statements. Estimates also affect the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the
reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates. The allowance for
doubtful accounts is a significant estimate used in the preparation of the accompanying
financial statements.

Cash and cash equivalents, escrow deposits and replacement reserve

The Home considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or
less to be cash equivalents. At December 31, 2019, the Home had no cash equivalents.

The Home maintains cash balances at various financial institutions in accounts insured by
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”). At December 31, 2019, these
balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $1,382,992.

The mortgagee holds the mortgage escrow deposits (noninterest-bearing) and the
replacement reserve (interest-bearing) in FDIC-insured accounts. At December 31, 2019,

these balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $263,264.

The Home monitors its concentration of deposits, including those held by the mortgagee, by
obtaining and evaluating bank ratings on a quarterly basis.

Receivables

Tenant accounts receivable and Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance reccivable are stated at
the amount the Home expects to collect.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Receivables (continued

Under Rhode Island General Law Title 40, Chapter 8, Section 6.1(b)(2), Human Services,
Medical Assistance, Provider Care During Pendency of Application, Uncompensated Care While
Determination is Overdue, upon the Home’s request, the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) is
required to make payments to the Home for charges related to a patient that the Home has
determined should be eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for
Medicaid benefits filed with the State has been pending for 90 days or more (“advance
payments”); such advance payments may not be recovered, offset or recouped by the State
upon a subsequent determination by the State that the patient is not eligible for Medicaid.
Consequently, advance payments received by the Home prior to the date the State has made
a determination related to the patient’s eligibility for Medicaid are offset against the tenant
accounts receivable included in the accompanying balance sheet. Advance payments received
by the Home related to Medicaid claims subsequently approved and paid by the State are
required to be repaid to the State through an ongoing reconciliation process and,
consequently, are reported within current liabilities, third-party advances in the
accompanying balance sheet. At December 31, 2019, advance payments offset against tenant
accounts receivable totaled $752,656.

The Home provides for probable uncollectible amounts through a charge to provision for
losses and a credit to the allowance for doubtful accounts based on its assessment of the
current status of individual accounts. Balances that are still outstanding after the Home has
used reasonable collection efforts are written off through a charge to the allowance for
doubtful accounts and a credit to receivables. The Home does not obtain collateral for
amounts due.

Approximately 16% and 6% of the Home’s tenant accounts receivable and
Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance receivable is due from the Rhode Island Medicaid and
federal Medicare programs, respectively.

At December 31, 2019 and 2018, accounts receivable was $2,976,773 and $2,243,594,
respectively.

Fixed assets

Fixed assets are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is provided
using the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets, ranging from 4
years to 40 years. Depreciation expense totaled $337,331, for the year ended December 31,
2019.

The Home evaluates long-lived assets held and used by the Home for impairment whenever
events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the asset may not be
recoverable.
