An impairment loss is recognized if the sum of the expected undiscounted future cash flows
from the use and disposition of the asset is less than its carrying amount. Generally, the
amount of impairment loss is measured as the difference between the carrying amount of the
asset and the estimated fair value of the asset. The Home did not record an impairment
loss during the year ended December 31, 2019.

Other asset

Nursing facility license fees are being amortized over the 33-year remaining life of the
building using the straight-line method. Amortization expense totaled $27,482 for the year
ended December 31, 2019.

Debt issuance costs

Debt issuance costs are being amortized over the 40-year term of the related mortgage note
obligation using the straight-line method, which approximates the effective interest method.
Amortization totaled $2,824 for the year ended December 31, 2019.

Income taxes

The Home has elected to be taxed as an S Corporation under the Internal Revenue
Code. Accordingly, the shareholders include the income or loss of the Home on their
respective income tax returns. In accordance with ASC 740, Income Taxes, the Home applies
the “more likely than not” threshold to the recognition and derecognition of tax positions
for its financial statements. Management has evaluated the Home’s tax positions and has
concluded that there were no uncertain tax positions that qualified for either recognition or
disclosure in these financial statements.

Revenue recognition

‘The Home adopted ASC Topic 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, on January 1, 2019.
Revenue is measured based on consideration specified in a contract with a customer, and
excludes any amounts collected on behalf of third parties. The Home recognizes revenue
when it satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control over a product or service
to a customer. The majority of the Home’s revenue originates from contracts with
customers to provide various healthcare services. The majority of the Home’s services
represent a bundle of services that are not capable of being distinct and as such, are treated
as a single performance obligation that is satisfied over time as the services are rendered. The
Home’s standard payment terms are within 30 days from billing.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Revenue recognition (continued)

The Home determines the transaction price based on contractually agreed upon rates,
adjusted for estimates of variable consideration, such as implicit price concessions. Variable
consideration also exists as the Home’s third-party revenue is paid principally at
prospectively determined rates. Retroactive adjustments are considered in the recognition of
revenue on an estimated basis in the period the related services are rendered such that net
patient service revenues are only recorded to the extent that it is probable that a significant
reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognized will not occur in the future. Any
differences between the estimated amounts accrued, and interim and final settlements are
adjusted in future periods as adjustments become known or as years ate no longer subject to
such audits, reviews and investigations.

Disaggregation of revenues

The Home operates as a skilled nursing facility and provides services to patients, principally
from Rhode Island, who have third-party financial coverage (principally Rhode Island
Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are responsible for their own
financial obligations. Therefore, the Home’s viability is dependent on a number of factors
such as licensed bed capacity, occupancy rates, mix of patient by payer and case type, the
rates of reimbursement, changes to Medicaid and Medicare programs, and the Home’s ability
to collect on its contracts. All of the Home’s net patient service revenue for financial
reporting purposes are recorded over time as the services are rendered.

Net patient service revenue from third-party payers totaled $15,065,572 for the year ended
December 31, 2019. Net patient service revenue from private payers totaled $2,732,775 for
the year ended December 31, 2019.

Significant risks and uncertainties

Laws and regulations governing Medicare, Medicaid and other governmental reimbursement
programs are extremely complex and subject to interpretation. As a result, there is at least a
reasonable possibility that recorded estimates could change by a material amount in the near
term. It is management’s opinion that the Home is in compliance with applicable laws and
regulations; however, the possibility of government review and interpretation exists.
Compliance with such laws and regulations can be subject to future government review and
interpretation, as well as significant regulatory action; failure to comply with such laws and
regulations can result in fines, penalties and exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid
programs.

NOTE 6. RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS

Management fee

The Home has a management agreement with Health Concepts, Ltd. (the “Home Office”), a
company owned by the shareholders, to provide home office services, principally
management services. The agreement expires in May 2032, unless automatically renewed for
an additional 15-year term in December 2031. The HUD-approved management fee is a
maximum of 7% of net patient service revenue. In 2019, management fees totaled 7% of net
patient service revenue, and amounted to $1,245,884 for the year ended December 31, 2019.

RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS (CONTINUED)

Workers’ compensation insurance

Effective January 1, 1994, the Home Office received permission from the Rhode Island
Department of Labor to establish a pooled self-insured workers’ compensation plan (the
“Plan”). The Home Office, the Home and eight nursing facilities owned by the Home’s
shareholders participate in the Plan and have transferred their workers’ compensation
insurance to the Plan.

The Plan provides for the payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as
well as payment for losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium
payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workers’ Compensation Trust (the
“Trust”) through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to establish a
cumulative reserve for future claims. The reserve is held in trust and invested by the Plan
trustee. The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a commercial insurance
cattier to protect the ‘T'rust’s assets from individual losses in excess of $450,000. In addition,
the Trust carries a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode Island Department of Labor,
collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a bank, for which no amounts are
outstanding at December 31, 2019.

The Trust Committee (the “Committee”) maintains separate accountability for each
participant’s portion of contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for
future claims. Should any participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs
and losses, the remaining participants’ portion of the Trust assets can be used to satisfy the
payments allocated to that participant. In the event of Plan termination, any assets
remaining in the Trust in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will
ultimately be returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares.

In the opinion of the Committee, the Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion
of current and estimated future costs, losses and future claims; accordingly, the Home’s
required premium for the year ended December 31, 2019, totaled $263,937, an amount that,
in management’s opinion, is below the premium it would pay to a commercial insurance
carrier if the Plan did not exist and did not achieve significant savings as a result of the loss
control program and monitoring services provided by the Home Office.

The Plan’s net assets at December 31, 2019, include cash and investments with a cost, which
approximates fair value, of $758,400 (unaudited).

Defined contribution plan

totaled $199,279 for the year ended December 31, 2019.

Health insurance

Effective January 1, 2018, the Home Office established a self-insured health insurance plan
(the “Health Plan”). The Home Office, the Home and other nursing facilities and a
business owned by the Home’s shareholders participate in the Health Plan and have
transferred their health insurance to the Health Plan. The Health Plan provides for the
payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as well as payment for losses.
Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium payments), as required, to the
Health Plan account maintained at the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to
establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The Health Plan carries excess loss
insurance coverage with a commercial insurance carrier to protect the Health Plan’s assets
from individual losses in excess of $100,000.

‘The Home Office maintains separate accountability for each participant’s portion of
contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for future claims. Should any
participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs, and losses, the remaining
participants’ portion of Health Plan assets can be used to satisfy the payments allocated to
that participant. In the event of Health Plan termination, any assets remaining in the Health
Plan in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will ultimately be returned
to the participants based on their pro rata shares. In the opinion of the Home Office, the
Health Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion of current and estimated future
costs, losses and future claims; the Home’s expense for the year ended December 31, 2019,
totaled $833,169.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS, COMMITMENT.
AND CONTINGENCIES

Medicaid eligibility determination delays

Since carly 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Home has determined should be eligible for
Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has been filed with
the State. The Home provides services to these patients and recognizes related revenue
during the period in which the State has not made a determination related to a completed
application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending Application”). Amounts reported as
tenant accounts receivable related to Medicaid Pending Applications that have been pending
for less than 90 days and those that have been pending for 90 days or more for which the
Home has not requested an advance payment (see Note 2) may be subject to subsequent
denial by the State at some future date. Management believes that the State will ultimately
determine that patients for whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are eligible for
Medicaid and that any potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently
denied by the State will not have a material adverse effect on the Home’s financial position.

Commitment

In a prior year, the Home was a party to a settlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Home paid an
agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement
agreement, the Home became a party to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with the
OIG. The CIA requires that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance
Program that promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled
nursing facilities affiliated with or owned, operated or managed by the Home Office,
including the Home. The CIA is for a five-year period commencing September 2016.
During the years ended December 31, 2017 and 2018, and in January 2020, the OIG
accepted the Annual Reports submitted by the Home Office pursuant to the CIA. The
Home Office is compliant with the requirements of the CIA as of December 31, 2019.

Continuing operations

The Home incurred a net loss in 2019, has incurred net losses in the past three years, and has
a shareholders’ deficiency. These conditions are significant to the Home’s ability to
continue operations and to meet its obligations. The Home has evaluated these conditions
and agreed with the Home Office to delay payment of accrued management fees owed to
the Home Office and to provide other support, as needed, allowing the Home the ability to
continue to operate and to meet its current obligations. This factor mitigates doubt about the
Home’s ability to continue as a going concern.

INDEPENDENT AUDITOR’S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL
REPORTING AND ON COMPLIANCE AND OTHER MATTERS BASED ON AN
AUDIT OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS PERFORMED IN ACCORDANCE WITH

GOVERNMENT AUDITING STANDARDS

To the Shareholders
Riverview Nursing Home Inc.
Coventry, Rhode Island

We have audited, in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America
and the standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards issued by the
Comptroller General of the United States, the financial statements of Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the
“Home”), which comprise the balance sheet as of December 31, 2019, and the related statements of
operations, shareholders’ deficiency and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related notes to the
financial statements, and have issued our report thereon dated April 15, 2020.

Internal Control over Financial Reporting

In planning and performing our audit of the financial statements, we considered the Home’s internal control

“over financial reporting (internal control) to determine the audit procedures that are appropriate in the
circumstances for the purpose of expressing our opinion on the financial statements, but not for the
purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal control. Accordingly, we do
not express an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal control.

A deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or
employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct,
misstatements on a timely basis. A material weakness is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in
internal control, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the entity’s
financial statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected on a timely basis. A significant deficiency
is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in internal control that is less severe than a matetial
weakness, yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance.

Our consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described in the first paragraph of this
section and was not designed to identify all deficiencies in internal control that might be material weaknesses
or significant deficiencies. Given these limitations, during our audit we did not identify any deficiencies in
internal control that we consider to be material weaknesses. However, material weaknesses may exist that
have not been identified.

Compliance and Other Matters

As part of obtaining reasonable assurance about whether the Home’s financial statements are free from
material misstatement, we performed tests of its compliance with certain provisions of laws, regulations,
contracts, and grant agreements, noncompliance with which could have a direct and material effect on the
determination of financial statement amounts. However, providing an opinion on compliance with those
provisions was not an objective of our audit and, accordingly, we do not express such an opinion. The
results of our tests disclosed no instances of noncompliance or other matters that are required to be
reported under Government Auditing Standards.

Purpose of this Report

The purpose of this report is solely to describe the scope of our testing of internal control and compliance
and the results of that testing, and not to provide an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal
control or on compliance. This report is an integral part of an audit performed in accordance with
Government Auditing Standards in considering the Home’s internal control and compliance. Accordingly, this
communication is not suitable for any other purpose.

Auditor’s Responsibility

Report on Internal Control over Compliance

Management of the Home is responsible for establishing and maintaining effective internal control over
compliance with the compliance requirements referred to above. In planning and performing our audit of
compliance, we considered the Home’s internal control over compliance with the requirements that could
have a direct and material effect on the major HUD program to determine the auditing procedures that are
appropriate in the circumstances for the purpose of expressing an opinion on compliance for the major
HUD program and to test and report on internal control over compliance in accordance with the audit
guide, but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control over
compliance. Accordingly, we do not express an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal
control over compliance.

A, deficiency in internal control over compliance exists when the design or operation of a control over compliance
does not allow management or employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to
prevent, or detect and correct, noncompliance with a compliance requirement of a HUD program on a
timely basis. A material weakness in internal control over compliance is a deficiency, or combination of deficiencics,
in internal control over compliance, such that there is a reasonable possibility that material noncompliance
with a compliance requirement of a HUD program will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a
timely basis. A significant deficiency in internal control over compliance is a deficiency, or a combination of
deficiencies, in internal control over compliance with a compliance requirement of a HUD program that is
less severe than a material weakness in internal control over compliance, yet important enough to merit
attention by those charged with governance.

Our consideration of internal control over compliance was for the limited purpose described in the first
paragraph of this section and was not designed to identify all deficiencies in internal control over
compliance that might be material weaknesses or significant deficiencies. We did not identify any
deficiencies in internal control over compliance that we consider to be material weaknesses. However,
material weaknesses may exist that have not been identified.

shareholders’ deficiency, and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related notes to the financial
statements.

Management is responsible for the preparation and fair presentation of these financial statements in accordance
with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America; this includes the design,
implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and fair presentation of financial
statements that ate free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud or error.

Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit. We conducted out
audit in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America and the standards
applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards, issued by the Comptroller General of the
United States. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements are free from material misstatement.

An audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the amounts and disclosures in the
financial statements. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment, including the assessment of the
tisks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud or error. In making those risk
assessments, the auditor considers internal control relevant to the entity’s preparation and fair presentation of the
financial statements in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the
purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the entity’s internal control. Accordingly, we express no
such opinion. An audit also includes evaluating the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the
reasonableness of significant accounting estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall
presentation of the financial statements.

We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our audit
opinion.

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS

Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the “Home”) d/b/a Riverview Healthcare Community, owns
and operates a 190-bed nursing facility located in Coventry, Rhode Island. The Home
provides services to patients, principally from Rhode Island, with third-party financial
coverage (principally Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are
responsible for their own financial obligations.

The Home is regulated by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
(“HUD”) as to operating methods under Section 232 of the National Housing Act of 1959
(the “Act”). The Section 232 Housing Program was formed under the Act and provides
HUD-insured mortgage notes to participating developments (see Note 4).

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
Use of estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”) requires management to make
estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, and
disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements.
Estimates also affect the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the reporting
period. Actual results could differ from those estimates. The allowance for doubtful
accounts is a significant estimate used in the preparation of the accompanying financial
statements.

Cash and cash equivalents, escrow deposits and replacement reserve

The Home considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or
less to be cash equivalents. At Decembet 31, 2020, the Home had no cash equivalents.

The Home maintains cash balances at various financial institutions in accounts insured by
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”). At December 31, 2020, these
balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $3,563,207.

The mortgagee holds the mortgage escrow deposits (noninterest-bearing) and the
replacement reserve (interest-bearing) in FDIC-insured accounts. At December 31, 2020,

these balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $217,054.

The Home monitors its concentration of deposits, including those held by the mortgagee, by
obtaining and evaluating bank ratings on a quarterly basis.

Receivables

Tenant accounts receivable and Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance receivable are stated at
the amount the Home expects to collect.

===== PAGE 1390 =====
[OCR]
NOTE 2.

RIVERVIEW NURSING HOME INC.
PROJECT NO. 016-43122

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Receivables (continued)

Under Rhode Island General Law Title 40, Chapter 8, Section 6.1(b)(2), Human Services,
Medical Assistance, Provider Care During Pendency of Application, Uncompensated Care While
Deterntination is Overdue, upon the Home’s request, the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) is
required to make payments to the Home for charges related to a patient that the Home has
determined should be eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for
Medicaid benefits filed with the State has been pending for 90 days or more (“advance
payments”); such advance payments may not be recovered, offset or recouped by the State
upon a subsequent determination by the State that the patient is not eligible for Medicaid.
Consequently, advance payments received by the Home prior to the date the State has made
a determination related to the patient’s eligibility for Medicaid are offset against the tenant
accounts receivable included in the accompanying balance sheet. Advance payments received
by the Home related to Medicaid claims subsequently approved and paid by the State are
required to be repaid to the State through an ongoing reconciliation process and,
consequently, are reported within current liabilities, third-party advances in the
accompanying balance sheet. At December 31, 2020, advance payments offset against tenant
accounts receivable totaled $736,769.

The Home provides for probable uncollectible amounts through a charge to provision for
losses and a credit to the allowance for doubtful accounts based on its assessment of the
current status of individual accounts. Balances that are still outstanding after the Home has
used reasonable collection efforts are written off through a charge to the allowance for
doubtful accounts and a credit to receivables. The Home does not obtain coilateral for
amounts due.

At December 31, 2020 and 2019, accounts receivable was $2,689,832 and $2,976,773,
respectively.

Fixed assets

Fixed assets are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is provided
using the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets, ranging from 4
years to 40 years. Depreciation expense totaled $339,085, for the year ended December 31,
2020.

‘The Home evaluates long-lived assets held and used by the Home for impairment whenever
events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the asset may not be
recoverable.

Fixed assets (continued)

An impairment loss is recognized if the sum of the expected undiscounted future cash flows
from the use and disposition of the asset is less than its carrying amount. Generally, the
amount of impairment loss is measured as the difference between the carrying amount of the
asset and the estimated fair value of the asset. The Home did not record an impairment
loss during the year ended December 31, 2020.

Other asset

Nursing facility license fees are being amortized over the 33-year remaining life of the
building using the straight-line method. Amortization expense totaled $27,482 for the year
ended December 31, 2020.

Debt issuance costs

Debt issuance costs are being amortized over the 40-year term of the related mortgage note
obligation using the straight-line method, which approximates the effective interest method.
Amortization totaled $2,890 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

Income taxes

The Home has elected to be taxed as an S Corporation under the Internal Revenue
Code. Accordingly, the shareholders include the income or loss of the Home on their
respective income tax returns. In accordance with Accounting Standards Codification
(“ASC”) 740, Income Taxes, the Home applies the “more likely than not” threshold to the
recognition and derecognition of tax positions for its financial statements. Management has
evaluated the Home’s tax positions and has concluded that there were no uncertain tax
positions that qualified for either recognition or disclosure in these financial statements.

Revenue recognition

Revenue is measured based on consideration specified in a contract with a customer, and
excludes any amounts collected on behalf of third parties. The Home recognizes revenue
when it satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control over a product or setvice
to a customer. The majority of the Home’s revenue originates from contracts with
customers to provide various healthcare services. The majority of the Home’s services
represent a bundle of services that are not capable of being distinct and as such, are treated
as a single performance obligation that is satisfied over time as the services are rendered. The
Home’s standard payment terms are within 30 days from billing.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Revenue recognition (continued)

The Home determines the transaction price based on contractually agreed upon rates,
adjusted for estimates of variable consideration, such as implicit price concessions. Variable
consideration also exists as the Home’s third-party revenue is paid principally at
prospectively determined rates. Retroactive adjustments are considered in the recognition of
revenue on an estimated basis in the period the related services are rendered such that net
patient service revenues are only recorded to the extent that it is probable that a significant
reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognized will not occur in the future. Any
differences between the estimated amounts accrued, and interim and final settlements are
adjusted in future periods as adjustments become known or as years are no longer subject to
such audits, reviews and investigations.

Disaggregation of revenues

The Home operates as a skilled nursing facility and provides services to patients, principally
from Rhode Island, who have third-party financial coverage (principally Rhode Island
Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are responsible for their own
financial obligations. Therefore, the Home’s viability is dependent on a number of factors
such as licensed bed capacity, occupancy rates, mix of patient by payer and case type, the
rates of reimbursement, changes to Medicaid and Medicare programs, and the Home’s ability
to collect on its contracts. All of the Home’s net patient service revenue for financial
reporting purposes are recorded over time as the services are rendered.

Net patient service revenue from third-party payers totaled $13,924,776 for the year ended
December 31, 2020. Net patient service revenue from private payers totaled $2,868,322 for
the year ended December 31, 2020.

Significant risks and uncertainties

Laws and regulations governing Medicare, Medicaid and other governmental reimbursement
programs are extremely complex and subject to interpretation. As a result, there is at least a
reasonable possibility that recorded estimates could change by a material amount in the near
term. It is management’s opinion that the Home is in compliance with applicable laws and
regulations; however, the possibility of government review and interpretation exists.
Compliance with such laws and regulations can be subject to future government review and
interpretation, as well as significant regulatory action; failure to comply with such laws and
regulations can result in fines, penalties and exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid
programs.

NOTE 6. OTHER LOAN AND NOTES PAYABLE AND SUBSEQUENT EVENT

On April 20, 2020, the Home received a loan in the amount of $1,971,100 under the
Paycheck Protection Program ("PPP") with its bank as part of the Small Business Act
(“SBA”). The PPP, which was established as part of the CARES Act, provides for loans to
qualifying businesses for amounts up to 2.5 times certain average monthly payroll expenses
of the qualifying business. The loans and accrued interest, or a portion thereof, may be
forgiven after twenty-four weeks so long as the borrower uses the loan proceeds for eligible
purposes, including payroll, benefits, rent, mortgage interest, and utilities, and maintains its
payroll levels. Not more than 40% of the amount forgiven can be attributable to non-payroll
costs. The PPP loan will be deferred until the SBA remits the loan forgiveness, if applicable,
to the lender.

15

===== PAGE 1396 =====
[OCR]
NOTE 6.

RIVERVIEW NURSING HOME INC.
PROJECT NO. 016-43122
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
DECEMBER 31, 2020

OTHER LOAN AND NOTES PAYABLE AND SUBSEQUENT EVENT
CONTINUED

The Home currently intends to use the proceeds for purposes consistent with the PPP,
however, there can be no assurances that the Home will ultimately meet the conditions for
forgiveness of the loan or that the Home will not take actions that could cause the

Home to be ineligible for forgiveness of the loan, in whole or in part.

U.S. GAAP does not contain authoritative accounting standards for forgivable loans
provided by governmental entities to a for profit entity. Absent authoritative accounting
standards, interpretative guidance issued and commonly applied by financial statement
preparers allow for the selection of accounting policies amongst acceptable
alternatives. Based on the facts and circumstances, the Home has determined it most
appropriate to account for the PPP loan proceeds under the debt model. The Home
deemed the debt model to be the most appropriate accounting policy for this arrangement as
the underlying PPP loan is a legal form of debt and there are significant contingencies
outside of the control of the Home, mainiy related to the third-party approval process for
forgiveness. Under the debt model, the Home recognizes the proceeds received as debt,
recognizes periodic interest expense in the period in which the interest accrues at the stated
interest rate and defers recognition of any potential forgiveness of the loan principal or
interest until the period in which the Home has been legally released for its obligation by the
lender. Accrued interest and principal payments on the loan will commence, at a maximum,
10 months after the end of the 24-weck covered period if the loan has not been forgiven in
full. ‘The loan matures two years from the date of first disbursement of proceeds to the
Home. If the PPP loan is not forgiven, the loan accrues interest from the date of
disbursement at 1%,

As of the date of this report, the PPP loan forgiveness has not been finalized. There can be
no assurance given that the Home will obtain forgiveness of the PPP Loan in whole or in
part. In order to apply for the PPP Loan, the Home certified that, among other things, the
current economic uncertainty made the PPP Loan request necessary to support its ongoing
operations. In addition, PPP loans under the CARES Act may be subject to certain rules,
regulations and procedures applicable to the SBA Loan Program, which includes PPP loans
under the CARES Act. The interpretation and applicability of these rules, regulations and
procedutes is unclear, as some of them have not been referenced in the CARES Act itself or
in the guidance and interpretations issued by the SBA to date. If it is determined that the
Home was not eligible to receive the PPP Loan, or that the Home has not adequately
complied with the rules, regulations and procedures applicable to the SBA’s Loan Program,
the Home could be subject to penalties and could be required to repay the PPP Loan in its
entirety.

UNEARNED CARES ACT FUNDS AND SUBSEQUENT EVENT

During the year ended December 31, 2020, the Home received Provider Relief Fund
(“PRP”) and Coronavirus Relief Fund (“CRF”) distributions, in the amounts of $1,147,482
and $335,605, respectively, provided for under the CARES Act from the HHS and the
Department of the ‘Treasury. ‘The distributions from the PRF and CRF are not subject to
repayment provided the Home is able to attest to and comply with the terms and conditions
of the funding, including demonstrating that the funds received have been used for
healthcare-related expenses or “lost revenues” (as defined by HHS) attributable to
COVID-19. Such funds under the PRF and CRF are recognized on a systematic and
rational basis once there is reasonable assurance that the applicable terms and conditions
required to retain the funds have been met. The Home continues to monitor compliance
with the terms and conditions of the PRF and CRF as the interpretations of these rules and
regulations are unclear and continue to be clarified. If it is determined that the use of funds
were not within the guidelines established by the PRF and CRF programs, the Home could
be required to repay these funds. For the year ended December 31, 2020, the Home
recorded $859,238 related to these submitted expenses and lost revenues in the statement of
loss as other revenue. As of December 31, 2020, $623,849 is recorded as prepaid income,
unearned CARES Act funds, in the accompanying balance sheet, as the eligible expenses had
not yet been incurred.

Subsequent to year end, the Home received additional PRF funding of approximately
$26,000.

UNCERTAINTY DUE TO COVID-19

In March 2020, the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak to
constitute a “Public Health Emergency of International Concern.” Disruptions to the
Home’s business operations occurted during 2020 and continue into 2021 as a result from
the supply and quarantine of employees, residents, and vendors. The Home, along with
most skilled nursing facilities throughout the U.S., has experienced a significant decline in
admissions and census and additional costs associated with retaining and attracting staff and
protective medical supplies due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Given the uncertainty of the
situation, an estimate of the financial impact to the Home, if any, cannot be reasonably
estimated at this time.

RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS

Management fee

The Home has a management agreement with Health Concepts, Ltd. (the “Home Office”), a
company owned by the shareholders, to provide home office services, principally
management services. The agreement expires in May 2032, unless automatically renewed for
an additional 15-year term in December 2031. The HUD-approved management fee is a
maximum of 7% of net patient service revenue. Management fees totaled 7% of net patient
service revenue, and amounted to $1,175,517 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS (CONTINUED)

Workers’ compensation insurance

Effective January 1, 1994, the Home Office received permission from the Rhode Island
Department of Labor to establish a pooled self-insured workers’ compensation plan (the
“Plan’). ‘The Home Office, the Home and eight nursing facilities owned by the Home’s
shareholders patticipate in the Plan and have transferred their workers’ compensation
insurance to the Plan.

The Plan provides for the payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as
well as payment for losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium
payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workers’ Compensation Trust (the
“Trust”) through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to establish a
cumulative reserve for future claims. ‘The reserve is held in trust and invested by the Plan
trustee. The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a commercial insurance
carrier to protect the Trust’s assets from individual losses in excess of $450,000. In addition,
the Trust carries a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode Island Department of Labor,
collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a bank, for which no amounts are
outstanding at December 31, 2020.

The ‘Trust Committee (the “Committee”) maintains separate accountability for each
patticipant’s portion of contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for
future claims. Should any participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs
and losses, the remaining participants’ portion of the Trust assets can be used to satisfy the
payments allocated to that participant. In the event of Plan termination, any assets
remaining in the ‘Itust in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will
ultimately be returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares.

In the opinion of the Committee, the Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion
of current and estimated futute costs, losses and future claims; accordingly, the Home’s
required premium for the year ended December 31, 2020, totaled $351,064, an amount that,
in management’s opinion, is below the premium it would pay to a commercial insurance
carrier if the Plan did not exist and did not achieve significant savings as a result of the loss
control program and monitoring services provided by the Home Office.

The Plan’s net assets at December 31, 2020, include cash and investments with a cost, which
approximates fair value, of $785,500 (unaudited).

RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS (CONTINUED)

Defined contribution plan

Effective November 1, 1996, the Home Office established a defined contribution plan,
Health Concepts, Ltd. 401(k) Plan, for the benefit of the employees of the Home Office, its
participating nursing facilities, and a business owned by the Home’s shareholders. The plan
covers all employees who meet the eligibility requirements, which include attainment of age
18 and the compietion of more than 999 hours of service in a prior year.

For 2020, the plan provides that the Home will match 75% of employee contributions up to
a maximum match of 7.5% of eligible compensation. The Home’s contributions to the plan
totaled $226,781 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

Health insurance

Effective January 1, 2018, the Home Office established a self-insured health insurance plan
(the “Health Plan”). The Home Office, the Home and other nursing facilities and a
business owned by the Home’s shareholders participate in the Health Plan and have
transferred their health insurance to the Health Plan. The Health Plan provides for the
payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as well as payment for losses.
Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium payments), as required, to the
Health Pian account maintained at the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to
establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The Health Plan carries excess loss
insurance coverage with a commercial insurance carrier to protect the Health Plan’s assets
from individual losses in excess of $100,000.

The Home Office maintains separate accountability for each participant's portion of
contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for future claims. Should any
participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs, and losses, the remaining
participants’ portion of Health Plan assets can be used to satisfy the payments allocated to
that participant. In the event of Health Plan termination, any assets remaining in the Health
Plan in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will ultimately be returned
to the participants based on their pro rata shares. In the opinion of the Home Office, the
Health Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion of current and estimated future
costs, losses and future claims; the Home’s expense for the year ended December 31, 2020,
totaled $844,481.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS, COMMITMENT
AND CONTINGENCIES

Medicaid eligibility determination delays

Since early 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Home has determined should be eligible for
Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has been filed with
the State. The Home provides services to these patients and recognizes related revenue
during the period in which the State has not made a determination related to a completed
application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending Application”). Amounts reported as
tenant accounts receivable related to Medicaid Pending Applications that have been pending
for less than 90 days and those that have been pending for 90 days or more for which the
Home has not requested an advance payment (see Note 2) may be subject to subsequent
denial by the State at some future date. Management believes that the State will ultimately
determine that patients for whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are eligible for
Medicaid and that any potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently
denied by the State will not have a material adverse effect on the Home’s financial position.

Commitment

In a ptior year, the Home was a party to a settlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Home paid an
agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement
agreement, the Home became a party to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with the
OIG. ‘The CIA requires that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance
Program that promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled
nursing facilities affiliated with or owned, operated or managed by the Home Office,
including the Home. The CIA is for a five-year period commencing September 2016.
During the years ended December 31, 2017 and 2018, and in January 2020 and January 2021,
the OIG accepted the Annual Reports submitted by the Home Office pursuant to the CIA.
The Home Office is compliant with the requirements of the CIA as of December 31, 2020.

Continuing operations

The Home incurred a net loss in 2020, has incurred net losses in past years, and has a
shareholders’ deficiency. These conditions are significant to the Home’s ability to continue
operations and to meet its obligations. The Home has evaluated these conditions and
agreed with the Home Office to delay payment of accrued management fees owed to the
Home Office, as needed, allowing the Home the ability to continue to operate and to meet
its current obligations, This factor, along with PPP and CARES Act funding received,
mitigates doubt about the Home’s ability to continue as a going concern.

INDEPENDENT AUDITOR’S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL

GOVERNMENT AUDITING STANDARDS

To the Shareholders
Riverview Nursing Home Inc.
Coventry, Rhode Island

We have audited, in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America
and the standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Aaditing Standards issued by the
Comptroller General of the United States, the financial statements of Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the
“Home”), which comprise the balance sheet as of December 31, 2020, and the related statements of loss,
shareholders’ deficiency and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related notes to the financial
statements, and have issued our report thereon dated June 23, 2021.

Internal Control over Financial Reporting

In planning and performing our audit of the financial statements, we considered the Home’s internal control
over financial reporting (internal control) as a basis for designing the audit procedures that are appropriate
in the circumstances for the purpose of expressing our opinion on the financial statements, but not for the
purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal control. Accordingly, we do
not express an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal control.

A deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or
employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct,
misstatements on a timely basis. A material weakness is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in
internal control, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the entity’s
financial statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected on a timely basis. A significant deficiency
is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in internal control that is less severe than a material
weakness, yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance.

Our consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described in the first paragraph of this
section and was not designed to identify all deficiencies in internal control that might be material weaknesses
or significant deficiencies. Given these limitations, during our audit we did not identify any deficiencies in
internal control that we consider to be material weaknesses. However, material weaknesses may exist that
have not been identified.

RIVERVIEW NURSING HOME INC.

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
DECEMBER 31, 2018

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS

Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the “Home”) d/b/a Riverview Healthcare Community, owns
and opetates a 190-bed nursing facility located in Coventry, Rhode Island. The Home
provides services to patients, principally from Rhode Island, with third-party financial
coverage (ptincipally Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are
responsible for their own financial obligations.

The Home is regulated by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
(“HUD”) as to operating methods under Section 232 of the National Housing Act of 1959
(the “Act”). The Section 232 Housing Program was formed undet the Act and provides
HUD-insured mortgage notes to participating developments (see Note 4).

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Recently issued but not yet effective accounting pronouncements

Revenue recognition

Jn May 2014, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) issued Accounting
Standards Update (“ASU”) No. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (Accounting
Standards Codification ("ASC") Topic 606), as amended (commonly referred to as "ASC
606"), which requires an entity to recognize revenue to depict the transfer of promised
goods or services to customers in an amount that reflects the consideration which the entity
expects to be entitled to receive in exchange for those goods or services. ASC 606 replaces
most existing revenue recognition standards in accounting principles generally accepted in
the United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”), including industry-specific standards, when it
becomes effective. For annual reporting periods, this standard is effective for the Home on
January 1, 2019, and for interim periods within annual periods that begin one year later.
The standard permits the use of either the retrospective or cumulative-effect transition
method. The Home is curtently completing its initial assessment and evaluation of the
impact that ASC 606 will have on the Home’s financial statements and related disclosures.

The Home expects to retrospectively adopt ASC 606 effective January 1, 2019. As a result,
substantially all amounts previously reported as provision for losses on patient services
receivables will now be considered an implicit price concession and will be recognized as a
reduction of net patient service revenue. The adoption of ASC 606 will also result in
expanded disclosures that will enable the users of the financial statements to better
understand the nature, amount, timing and uncertainty, if any, of revenues and cash flows
arising from contracts with customers.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Recently issued but not yet effective accounting pronouncements (continued

Statement of cash flows

In November 2016, the FASB issued ASU No. 2016-18, Statement of Cash Flows (Topic 230):
Restricted Cash (a consensus of the Emerging Issues Task Force) (“ASU 2016-18”), which requires an
entity to present restricted cash and cash equivalents together with unrestricted cash and
cash equivalents in the statement of cash flows. Under ASU 2016-18, an entity will be
required to disclose in the financial statements how the statement of cash flows reconciles to
the balance sheet, if restricted cash and cash equivalents ate presented separate from
unrestricted cash and cash equivalents on the balance sheet, and the nature of the restrictions
at the balance sheet date. This new guidance is effective for years beginning after
December 15, 2018, with early adoption permitted. Upon adoption of the amendments in
ASU 2016-18, the Home will present within the statement of cash flows the change during
the period in total cash and cash equivalents, including amounts generally described as
restricted cash and cash equivalents. The amendments will be applied retrospectively.

Use of estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP tequires
management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets
and liabilities, and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial
statements. Estimates also affect the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the
reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates. The allowance for
doubtful accounts is a significant estimate used in the preparation of the accompanying
financial statements.

Cash and cash equivalents, esctow deposits and replacement reserve

The Home considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or
less to be cash equivalents. At December 31, 2018, the Home had no cash equivalents.

‘The Home maintains cash balances at vatious financial institutions in accounts insured by
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”). At December 31, 2018, these
balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $1,850,882.

The mortgagee holds the mortgage escrow deposits (noninterest-bearing) and the
replacement reserve (interest-bearing) in FDIC-insured accounts. At December 31, 2018,
these balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $413,035.

The Home monitors its concentration of deposits, including those held by the mortgagee, by
obtaining and evaluating bank ratings on a quarterly basis.

Receivables

Tenant accounts receivable and Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance receivable are stated at
the amount the Home expects to collect.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)
Receivables (continued)

Under Rhode Island General Law Title 40, Chapter 8, Section 6.1(b)(2) , Human Services,
Medical Assistance, Provider Care During Pendency of Application, Uncompensated Care While
Determination is Overdue, upon the Home’s request, the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) is
tequired to make payments to the Home for charges related to a patient that the Home has
determined should be eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for
Medicaid benefits filed with the State has been pending for 90 days or more (“advance
payments”); such advance payments may not be recovered, offset or recouped by the State
upon a subsequent determination by the State that the patient is not eligible for Medicaid.
Consequently, advance payments received by the Home prior to the date the State has made
a determination related to the patient’s cligibility for Medicaid are offset against the tenant
accounts receivable included in the accompanying balance sheet. Advance payments teceived
by the Home related to Medicaid claims subsequently approved and paid by the State are
requited to be tepaid to the State through an ongoing reconciliation process and,
consequently, are reported within current liabilities, third-party advances in the
accompanying balance sheet. At December 31, 2018, advance payments offset against tenant
receivables totaled $1,397,970.

The Home provides for probable uncollectible amounts through a charge to provision for
losses and a credit to the allowance for doubtful accounts based on ‘its assessment of the
current status of individual accounts. Balances that are still outstanding after the Home has
used reasonable collection efforts are written off through a charge to the allowance for
doubtful accounts and a credit to receivables. The Home does not obtain collateral for
amounts due.

Approximately 13% and 5% of the Home’s tenant accounts receivable and
Medicate/Medicaid/other insurance receivable is due from the Rhode Island Medicaid and
federal Medicare programs, respectively.

Fixed assets

Fixed assets are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is provided
using the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets, ranging from 4
years to 40 yeats. Depreciation expense totaled $350,264 for the year ended December 31,
218.

The Home evaluates long-lived assets held and used by the Home for impairment whenever
events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the asset may not be
recoverable. An impairment loss is recognized if the sum of the expected undiscounted
future cash flows from the use and disposition of the asset is less than its carrying amount.
Generally, the amount of impairment loss is measured as the difference between the carrying
amount of the asset and the estimated fair value of the asset. The Home did not record an
impairment loss during the year ended Decembet 31, 2018.

Income taxes

disclosure in these financial statements.

Net patient service revenue

Net patient service revenue is reported at estimated net amounts realizable from residents,

services rendered.

The Home’s third-party revenue is paid principally at prospectively determined rates.

in the period the related services are rendered; any differences between the estimated
amounts accrued, and interim and final settlements are adjusted in future petiods as
adjustments become known or as years are no longer subject to such audits, reviews and
investigations.

RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS

Management fee

The Home has a management agreement with Health Concepts, Ltd. (the “Home Office”), a
company owned by the shareholders, to provide home office services, principally
management services. The agreement expires in May 2032, unless automatically renewed for
an additional 15-year term in December 2031. The HUD-approved management fee is a
maximum of 7% of net patient service revenue. In 2018, management fees totaled 6% of net
patient service revenue, and amounted to $1,007,445 for the year ended December 31, 2018.

Workers’ compensation insurance

Effective January 1, 1994, the Home Office received permission from the Rhode Island
Department of Labor to establish a pooled self-insured workers’ compensation plan (the
“Plan”). The Home Office, the Home and eight nursing facilities owned by the Home’s
shareholders participate in the Plan and have transferred their workers’ compensation
insurance to the Plan.

The Plan provides for the payment of administiation, claims and tisk management costs, as
well as payment for losses. Tach participant makes monthly contributions (premium
payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workers’ Compensation Trust (the _
“Trust”) through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to establish a
cumulative reserve for future claims. The reserve is held in trust and invested by the Plan
trustee. The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a commetcial insurance
cartier to protect the Trust’s assets from individual losses in excess of $450,000. In addition,
the Trust carries a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode Island Department of Labor,
collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a bank, for which no amounts are
outstanding at December 31, 2018.

The Trust Committee (the “Committee”) maintains separate accountability for each
patticipant’s portion of contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for
future claims. Should any patticipant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs
and losses, the remaining participants’ portion of the Trust assets can be used to satisfy the
payments allocated to that participant. In the event of Plan termination, any assets
remaining in the Trust in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will
ultimately be returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares.

In the opinion of the Committee, the Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion
of current and estimated future costs, losses and future claims; accordingly, the Home’s
required premium for the year ended December 31, 2018, totaled $263,937, an amount that,
in management’s opinion, is below the premium it would pay to a commercial insurance
carrier if the Plan did not exist and did not achieve significant savings as a result of the loss
control program and monitoring services provided by the Home Office.

Defined contribution plan

Effective November 1, 1996, the Home Office established a defined contribution plan,
Health Concepts, Ltd. 401(k) Plan, for the benefit of the employees of the Home Office, its
patticipating nursing facilities, and a business owned by the Home’s shareholders. The plan
covers all employees who mect the eligibility requirements, which include attainment of age
18 and the completion of more than 999 hours of service in a prior year. The Home Office,

the Home and ten nursing facilities owned by the Home’s shareholders participate in the
plan.

For 2018, the plan provides that the Home will match 75% of employee contributions up to
a maximum match of 7.5% of eligible compensation. ‘The Home’s contributions to the plan
totaled $215,657 for the year ended December 31, 2018.

Health insurance

Effective January 1, 2018, the Home Office established a self-insured health insurance plan
(the “Health Plan”). The Home Office, the Home and other nursing facilities and a
business owned by the Home’s shareholders participate in the Health Plan and have
transferred their health insurance to the Health Plan. The Health Plan provides for the
payment of administration, claims and tisk management costs, as well as payment fot losses.
Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium payments), as required, to the
Health Plan account maintained at the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to
establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The Health Plan carries excess loss
insurance coverage with a commercial insurance carrier to protect the Health Plan’s assets
from individual losses in excess of $100,000.

The Home Office maintains separate accountability for each participant’s portion of
contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for future claims. Should any
participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs, and losses, the remaining
participants’ portion of Health Plan assets can be used to satisfy the payments allocated to
that participant. In the event of Health Plan tetmination, any assets remaining in the Health
Plan in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will ultimately be returned
to the participants based on their pro rata shares. In the opinion of the Home Office, the
Health Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion of current and estimated future
costs, losses and future claims; the Home’s expense for the year ended December 31, 2018,
totaled $792,438.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS, COMMITMENT
AND CONTINGENCIES

Medicaid eligibility determination delays

Since early 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Home has determined should be eligible for
Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has been filed with
the State. ‘The Home provides services to these patients and recognizes related revenue
during the period in which the State has not made a determination related to a completed
application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending Application”). Amounts reported as
tenant accounts receivable related to Medicaid Pending Applications that have been pending
for less than 90 days and those that have been pending for 90 days or more for which the
Home has not requested an advance payment (see Note 2) may be subject to subsequent
denial by the State at some future date. Management believes that the State will ultimately
determine that patients for whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are eligible for
Medicaid and that any potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently
denied by the State will not have a material adverse effect on the Home’s financial position.

Commitment

In a prior year, the Home was a party to a settlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Home paid an
agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement
agreement, the Home became a party to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with the
OIG. The CIA requires that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance
Program that promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled
nursing facilities affiliated with or owned, operated or managed by the Home Office,
including the Home. The CIA is for a five-year period commencing September 2016.
During the year ended December 31, 2017, the OIG accepted the Annual Report submitted
by the Home Office pursuant to the CIA. The Home Office is compliant with the
requirements of the CIA as of December 31, 2018.

Continuing operations

The Home incurted a net loss in 2018, has incurred net losses in the past two years, has a
shareholdets’ deficiency and a working capital ratio of less than 1.0. These conditions are
significant to the Home’s ability to continue operations and to meet its obligations. The
Home has evaluated these conditions and agreed with the Home Office to delay payment of
accrued management fees owed to the Home Office, as needed, allowing the Home the
ability to continue to operate and to meet its current obligations. This factor mitigates doubt
about the Home’s ability to continue as a going concern.

Internal Control over Financial Reporting

over financial reporting (internal control) to determine the audit procedures that are appropriate in the
circumstances for the purpose of expressing our opinion on the financial statements, but not for the

A deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or
employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, ot detect and correct,
misstatements on a timely basis. A material weakness is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in
internal control, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the entity’s
financial statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected on a timely basis. A significant deficiency
is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in internal control that is less severe than a material
weakness, yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance.

Our consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described in the first paragraph of this
section and was not designed to identify all deficiencies in internal control that might be material weaknesses
or significant deficiencies. Given these limitations, during our audit we did not identify any deficiencies in
internal control that we consider to be material weaknesses. However, material weaknesses may exist that
have not been identified.

NOTE 1.

NOTE 2.

RIVERVIEW NURSING HOME INC.
PROJECT NO. 016-43122
NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
DECEMBER 31, 2019

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS

Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the “Home”) d/b/a Riverview Healthcare Community, owns
and operates a 190-bed nursing facility located in Coventry, Rhode Island. The Home
provides services to patients, principally from Rhode Island, with third-party financial
coverage (principally Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are
responsible for their own financial obligations.

The Home is regulated by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
(HUD?) as to operating methods under Section 232 of the National Housing Act of 1959
(the “Act”). The Section 232 Housing Program was formed under the Act and provides
HUD-insured mortgage notes to participating developments (see Note 4).

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Recently adopted accounting pronouncements

Revenue recognition

In May 2014, the Financial Accounting Standards Board (“FASB”) issued Accounting
Standards Update (“ASU”) No. 2014-09, Revenue from Contracts with Customers (“Topic 606”),
with several clarifying updates issued subsequently. In conjunction with Topic 606, a new
subtopic, Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) 340-40, Other Assets and Deferred Costs —
Contracts with Customers, was also issued. The updated standard replaces most existing revenue
recognition and certain cost guidance under accounting principles generally accepted in the
United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”). Collectively, we refer to Topic 606 and Subtopic
340-40 as “ASC 606”. ASC 606 amends existing accounting standards for revenue
recognition and establishes principles for recognizing revenue upon the transfer of promised
goods or services to customets based on the expected consideration to be received in
exchange for those goods and services. The Home adopted ASC 606 effective January 1,
2019 using the modified retrospective transition method. The Home has determined that the
adjustments using the modified retrospective approach did not have a material impact on the
date of the initial application. The Home did not apply any practical expedients in
implementing ASC 606.

Restricted cash

In November 2016, FASB issued ASU No. 2016-18, Statement of Cash Flows (Topic 230):
Restricted Cash (‘ASU 2016-18”), which required that restricted cash and restricted cash
equivalents be included with cash and cash equivalents when reconciling the
beginning-of-period and end-of-period total amounts shown on the statement of cash flows.
ASU 2016-18 was effective for annual periods beginning after December 15, 2018 and
interim petiods within fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2019.

Use of estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with U.S. GAAP requires
management to make estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets
and liabilities, and disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial
statements. Estimates also affect the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the
reporting period. Actual results could differ from those estimates. The allowance for
doubtful accounts is a significant estimate used in the preparation of the accompanying
financial statements.

Cash and cash equivalents, escrow deposits and replacement reserve

The Home considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or
less to be cash equivalents. At December 31, 2019, the Home had no cash equivalents.

The Home maintains cash balances at various financial institutions in accounts insured by
the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”). At December 31, 2019, these
balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $1,382,992.

The mortgagee holds the mortgage escrow deposits (noninterest-bearing) and the
replacement reserve (interest-bearing) in FDIC-insured accounts. At December 31, 2019,

these balances exceeded the FDIC-insured limits by $263,264.

The Home monitors its concentration of deposits, including those held by the mortgagee, by
obtaining and evaluating bank ratings on a quarterly basis.

Receivables

Tenant accounts receivable and Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance receivable ate stated at
the amount the Home expects to collect.

10

===== PAGE 1483 =====
[OCR]
NOTE 2.

RIVERVIEW NURSING HOME INC.

NOTES TO FINANCIAL STATEMENTS
DECEMBER 31, 2019

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)
Receivables (continued)

Under Rhode Island General Law Title 40, Chapter 8, Section 6.1(b)(2), Human Services,
Medical Assistance, Provider Care During Pendency of Application, Uncompensated Care While
Determination is Overdue, upon the Home’s request, the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) is
required to make payments to the Home for charges related to a patient that the Home has
determined should be eligible for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for
Medicaid benefits filed with the State has been pending for 90 days or more (“advance
payments”); such advance payments may not be recovered, offset or recouped by the State
upon a subsequent determination by the State that the patient is not eligible for Medicaid.
Consequently, advance payments received by the Home prior to the date the State has made
a determination related to the patient’s eligibility for Medicaid are offset against the tenant
accounts receivable included in the accompanying balance sheet. Advance payments received
by the Home related to Medicaid claims subsequently approved and paid by the State are
required to be repaid to the State through an ongoing reconciliation process and,
consequently, are reported within current liabilities, third-party advances in the
accompanying balance sheet. At December 31, 2019, advance payments offset against tenant
accounts receivable totaled $752,656.

The Home provides for probable uncollectible amounts through a charge to provision for
losses and a credit to the allowance for doubtful accounts based on its assessment of the
current status of individual accounts. Balances that are still outstanding after the Home has
used reasonable collection efforts are written off through a charge to the allowance for
doubtful accounts and a credit to receivables. The Home does not obtain collateral for
amounts due.

Approximately 16% and 6% of the Home’s tenant accounts receivable and
Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance receivable is due from the Rhode Island Medicaid and
federal Medicare programs, respectively.

At December 31, 2019 and 2018, accounts receivable was $2,976,773 and $2,243,594,
respectively.

Fixed assets

Fixed assets are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is provided
using the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets, ranging from 4

yeats to 40 years. Depreciation expense totaled $337,331, for the year ended December 31,
2019.

The Home evaluates long-lived assets held and used by the Home for impairment whenever
events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the asset may not be
recoverable.

Fixed assets (continued)

An impairment loss is recognized if the sum of the expected undiscounted future cash flows
from the use and disposition of the asset is less than its carrying amount. Generally, the
amount of impairment loss is measured as the difference between the carrying amount of the
asset and the estimated fair value of the asset. The Home did not record an impairment
loss during the year ended December 31, 2019.

Other asset

Nursing facility license fees are being amortized over the 33-year remaining life of the
building using the straight-line method. Amortization expense totaled $27,482 for the year
ended December 31, 2019.

Debt issuance costs

Debt issuance costs are being amortized over the 40-year term of the related mortgage note
obligation using the straight-line method, which approximates the effective interest method.
Amortization totaled $2,824 for the year ended December 31, 2019.

Income taxes

The Home has elected to be taxed as an S Corporation under the Internal Revenue
Code. Accordingly, the shareholders include the income or loss of the Home on their
respective income tax returns. In accordance with ASC 740, Income Taxes, the Home applies
the “more likely than not” threshold to the recognition and detecognition of tax positions
for its financial statements. Management has evaluated the Home’s tax positions and has
concluded that there were no uncertain tax positions that qualified for either recognition or
disclosure in these financial statements.

Revenue recognition

The Home adopted ASC Topic 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers, on January 1, 2019.
Revenue is measured based on consideration specified in a contract with a customer, and
excludes any amounts collected on behalf of third parties. The Home tecognizes revenue
when it satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control over a product or service
to a customer. The majority of the Home’s revenue originates from contracts with
customers to provide various healthcare services. The majority of the Home’s services
represent a bundle of setvices that are not capable of being distinct and as such, are treated
as a single performance obligation that is satisfied over time as the services are rendered. The
Home’s standard payment terms are within 30 days from billing.

12

===== PAGE 1485 =====
[OCR]
NOTE 2.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)
Revenue recognition (continued

The Home determines the transaction price based on contractually agreed upon rates,
adjusted for estimates of variable consideration, such as implicit price concessions. Variable
consideration also exists as the Home’s third-party revenue is paid principally at
ptospectively determined rates. Retroactive adjustments are considered in the recognition of
revenue on an estimated basis in the period the related services are rendered such that net
patient service revenues ate only recorded to the extent that it is probable that a significant
reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognized will not occur in the future. Any
differences between the estimated amounts accrued, and interim and final settlements are
adjusted in future periods as adjustments become known ot as years ate no longer subject to
such audits, reviews and investigations.

Disaggregation of revenues

The Home operates as a skilled nursing facility and provides services to patients, principally
from Rhode Island, who have third-party financial coverage (principally Rhode Island
Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are responsible for their own
financial obligations. Therefore, the Home’s viability is dependent on a number of factors

-such as licensed bed capacity, occupancy rates, mix of patient by payer and case type, the

rates of reimbursement, changes to Medicaid and Medicare programs, and the Home’s ability
to collect on its contracts. All of the Home’s net patient service revenue for financial
reporting purposes are recorded over time as the services are rendered.

Net patient service revenue from third-party payers totaled $15,065,572 for the year ended
December 31, 2019. Net patient service revenue from private payers totaled $2,732,775 for
the year ended December 31, 2019.

Significant risks and uncertainties

Laws and regulations governing Medicare, Medicaid and other governmental reimbursement
programs are extremely complex and subject to interpretation. As a result, there is at least a
reasonable possibility that recorded estimates could change by a material amount in the near
term. It is management’s opinion that the Home is in compliance with applicable laws and
regulations, however, the possibility of government review and interpretation exists.
Compliance with such laws and regulations can be subject to future government review and
interpretation, as well as significant regulatory action; failure to comply with such laws and
regulations can result in fines, penalties and exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid
programs.

NOTE 6. RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS

Management fee

The Home has a management agreement with Health Concepts, Ltd. (the “Home Office”), a
company owned by the shareholders, to provide home office services, principally
management services. The agreement expires in May 2032, unless automatically renewed for
an additional 15-year term in December 2031. The HUD-approved management fee is a
maximum of 7% of net patient service revenue. In 2019, management fees totaled 7% of net
patient service revenue, and amounted to $1,245,884 for the yeat ended December 31, 2019.
