RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS (CONTINUED)

Workers’ compensation insurance

Effective January 1, 1994, the Home Office teceived permission from the Rhode Island
Department of Labor to establish a pooled self-insured workers’ compensation plan (the
“Plan”). The Home Office, the Home and eight nursing facilities owned by the Home’s
shareholders participate in the Plan and have transferred their workers’ compensation
insurance to the Plan.

The Plan provides for the payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as
well as payment for losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium
payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workets’? Compensation Trust (the
“Trust”) through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to establish a
cumulative reserve for future claims. The reserve is held in trust and invested by the Plan
trustee. The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a commercial insurance
carrict to protect the Trust’s assets from individual losses in excess of $450,000. In addition,
the Trust carries a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode Island Department of Labor,
collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a bank, for which no amounts ate
outstanding at December 31, 2019.

The Trust Committee (the “Committee”) maintains sepatate accountability for each
patticipant’s portion of contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for
future claims. Should any participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs
and losses, the remaining participants’ portion of the Trust assets can be used to satisfy the
payments allocated to that participant. In the event of Plan termination, any assets
remaining in the Trust in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will
ultimately be returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares.

In the opinion of the Committee, the Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion
of current and estimated future costs, losses and future claims; accordingly, the Home’s
required ptemium for the year ended December 31, 2019, totaled $263,937, an amount that,
in management’s opinion, is below the premium it would pay to a commercial insurance
cattier if the Plan did not exist and did not achieve significant savings as a result of the loss
control program and monitoring services provided by the Home Office.

The Plan’s net assets at December 31, 2019, include cash and investments with a cost, which
approximates fair value, of $758,400 (unaudited).

Defined contribution plan

Effective November 1, 1996, the Home Office established a defined contribution plan,
Health Concepts, Ltd. 401(k) Plan, for the benefit of the employees of the Home Office, its
participating nursing facilities, and a business owned by the Home’s shareholders. The plan
covers all employees who meet the eligibility requirements, which include attainment of age
18 and the completion of more than 999 hours of service in a prior year. ‘The Home Office,
the Home and ten nursing facilities owned by the Home’s shareholders participate in the
plan.

For 2019, the plan provides that the Home will match 75% of employee contributions up to
a maximum’match of 7.5% of eligible compensation. The Home’s contributions to the plan
totaled $199,279 for the year ended December 31, 2019.

Health insurance

Effective January 1, 2018, the Home Office established a self-insured health insurance plan
(the “Health Plan”). The Home Office, the Home and other nursing facilities and a
business owned by the Home’s shareholders participate in the Health Plan and have
transferred their health insurance to the Health Plan. The Health Plan provides for the
payment of administration, claims and tisk management costs, as well as payment for losses.
Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium payments), as required, to the
Health Plan account maintained at the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to
establish a cumulative reserve for future claims. The Health Plan carries excess loss
insurance coverage with a commercial insurance carrier to protect the Health Plan’s assets
from individual losses in excess of $100,000.

The Home Office maintains separate accountability for each participant’s portion of
contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for future claims. Should any
participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs, and losses, the remaining
participants’ portion of Health Plan assets can be used to satisfy the payments allocated to
that participant. In the event of Health Plan termination, any assets remaining in the Health
Plan in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will ultimately be returned
to the participants based on their pro rata shares. In the opinion of the Home Office, the
Health Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion of current and estimated future
costs, losses and future claims; the Home’s expense for the year ended December 31, 2019,
totaled $833,169.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS, COMMITMENT
AND CONTINGENCIES

Medicaid eligibility determination delays

Since early 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Home has determined should be eligible for
Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has been filed with
the State. The Home provides services to these patients and recognizes related revenue
during the period in which the State has not made a determination related to a completed
application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending Application”). Amounts reported as
tenant accounts receivable related to Medicaid Pending Applications that have been pending
for less than 90 days and those that have been pending for 90 days or more for which the
Home has not requested an advance payment (see-Note 2) may be subject to subsequent
denial by the State at some future date. Management believes that the State will ultimately
determine that patients for whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are eligible for
Medicaid and that any potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently
denied by the State will not have a material adverse effect on the Home’s financial position.

Commitment

In a prior year, the Home was a party to a settlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Home paid an
agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement
agreement, the Home became a party to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with the
OIG. The CIA tequires that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance
Program that promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled
nursing facilities affiliated with or owned, operated or managed by the Home Office,
including the Home. The CIA is for a five-yeat period commencing September 2016.
During the years ended December 31, 2017 and 2018, and in January 2020, the OIG
accepted the Annual Reports submitted by the Home Office pursuant to the CIA. The
Home Office is compliant with the requirements of the CIA as of December 31, 2019.

Continuing operations

The Home incurred a net loss in 2019, has incurted net losses in the past three years, and has
a shareholders’ deficiency. These conditions ate significant to the Home’s ability to
continue operations and to meet its obligations. The Home has evaluated these conditions
and agreed with the Home Office to delay payment of accrued management fees owed to
the Home Office and to provide other support, as needed, allowing the Home the ability to
continue to operate and to meet its current obligations. This factor mitigates doubt about the
Home’s ability to continue as a going concern.

INDEPENDENT AUDITOR’S REPORT ON INTERNAL CONTROL OVER FINANCIAL
REPORTING AND ON COMPLIANCE AND OTHER MATTERS BASED ON AN
AUDIT OF FINANCIAL STATEMENTS PERFORMED IN ACCORDANCE WITH

GOVERNMENT AUDITING STANDARDS

To the Shareholders
Riverview Nursing Home Inc.
Coventry, Rhode Island

We have audited, in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of Ametica
and the standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards issued by the
Comptroller General of the United States, the financial statements of Riverview Nursing Home Inc. (the
“Home”), which comprise the balance sheet as of December 31, 2019, and the related statements of
operations, shareholders’ deficiency and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related notes to the
financial statements, and have issued our report thereon dated April 15, 2020.

Internal Control over Financial Reporting

in planning and performing our audit of the financial statements, we considered the Home’s internal control
over financial reporting (internal control) to determine the audit procedures that are approptiate in the
circumstances for the purpose of expressing our opinion on the financial statements, but not for the
purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal control. Accordingly, we do
not express an opinion on the effectiveness of the Home’s internal control.

A. deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or
employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct,
misstatements on a timely basis. A material weakness is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in
internal control, such that thete is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the entity’s
financial statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected on a timely basis. A significant deficiency
is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in internal control that is less severe than a material
weakness, yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance.

Our consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described in the first paragraph of this
section and was not designed to identify all deficiencies in internal control that might be material weaknesses
or significant deficiencies. Given these limitations, during our audit we did not identify any deficiencies in
internal control that we consider to be material weaknesses. However, material weaknesses may exist that
have not been identified.

Management’s Responsibility for the Financial Statements

with accounting principles generally accepted in the United States of America; this includes the design,
implementation, and maintenance of internal control relevant to the preparation and fair presentation of financial
statements that are free from material misstatement, whether due to fraud ot error.

Auditor’s Responsibility

Our responsibility is to express an opinion on these financial statements based on our audit. We conducted our
audit in accordance with auditing standatds generally accepted in the United States of Ametica and the standards
applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards, issued by the Comptroller Genetal of the
United States. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about
whether the financial statements are free from material misstatement.

An audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit evidence about the amounts and disclosutes in the
financial statements. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s judgment, including the assessment of the
risks of material misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to fraud or error. In making those risk
assessments, the auditor considers internal control relevant to the entity’s preparation and fair presentation of the
financial statements in order to design audit procedures that are appropriate in the circumstances, but not for the
purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the entity’s internal control. Accordingly, we express no
such opinion. An audit also includes evaluating the appropriateness of accounting policies used and the
reasonableness of significant accounting estimates made by management, as well as evaluating the overall
presentation of the financial statements.

DESCRIPTION OF BUSINESS

Westerly Health Center Associates, L.P. (a Limited Partnership) (the “Partnership”) owns and
operates a 120-bed nursing facility located in Westerly, Rhode Island, of which 106 beds were
in service during 2020. The Partnership provides services to patients, principally from Rhode
Island, with third-party financial coverage (principally Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to
other patients who are responsible for their own financial obligations.

The Partnership is regulated by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development
(“HUD”) as to operating methods under Section 232 of the National Housing Act of 1959
(the “Act”). The Section 232 Housing Program was formed under the Act and provides
HUD-insured mortgage notes to participating developments (see Note 3).

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES

Use of estimates

The preparation of financial statements in conformity with accounting principles generally
accepted in the United States of America (“U.S. GAAP”) requites management to make
estimates and assumptions that affect the reported amounts of assets and liabilities, and
disclosure of contingent assets and liabilities at the date of the financial statements. Estimates
also affect the reported amounts of revenue and expenses during the reporting period. Actual
results could differ from those estimates. The allowance for doubtful accounts is a significant
estimate used in the preparation of the accompanying financial statements.

Cash and cash equivalents, escrow deposits and replacement reserve

The Partnership considers all highly liquid investments with original maturities of three
months or less to be cash equivalents. At December 31, 2020, the Partnership had no cash
equivalents.

The Partnership maintains cash balances at various financial institutions in accounts insured
by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (“FDIC”) and National Credit Union
Administration (“NCUA”). At December 31, 2020, these balances exceeded the insured limits
by $3,103,100.

The mortgagee holds the mortgage escrow deposits (noninterest-bearing) and the replacement
reserve (interest-bearing) in FDIC-insured accounts. At December 31, 2020, these balances
exceeded the insured limits by $123,516.

The Partnership monitors its concentration of deposits, including those held by the mortgagee,
by obtaining and evaluating bank ratings on a quarterly basis.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Receivables

Tenant accounts receivable and Medicare/Medicaid/other insurance receivable are stated at
the amount the Partnership expects to collect.

Under Rhode Island General Law Title 40, Chapter 8, Section 6.1(b)(2) , Human Services, Medical
Assistance, Provider Care During Pendency of Application, Uncompensated Care While Determination is
Overdue, upon the Partnership’s request, the State of Rhode Island (the “State”) is required to
make payments to the Partnership for charges related to a patient that the Partnership has
determined should be eligible for Medicaid and for whom a compieted application for
Medicaid benefits filed with the State has been pending for 90 days or more (“advance
payments”); such advance payments may not be recovered, offset or recouped by the State
upon a subsequent determination by the State that the patient is not eligible for Medicaid.
Consequently, advance payments received by the Partnership prior to the date the State has
made a determination related to the patient’s eligibility for Medicaid are offset against the
tenant accounts receivable included in the accompanying balance sheet. Advance payments
received by the Partnership related to Medicaid claims subsequently approved and paid by the
State are required to be repaid to the State through an ongoing reconciliation process and,
consequently, are reported within current liabilities, third-party advances in the accompanying
balance sheet. At December 31, 2020, advance payments offset against tenant accounts
receivable totaled $39,935.

The Partnership provides for probable uncollectible amounts through a charge to provision
for losses and a credit to the allowance for doubtful accounts based on its assessment of the
current status of individual accounts. Balances that arc still outstanding after the Partnership
has used reasonable collection efforts are written off through a charge to the allowance for
doubtful accounts and a credit to receivables. The Partnership does not obtain collateral for
amounts due.

At December 31, 2020 and 2019, accounts receivable was $870,757 and $968,801, respectively.
Fixed assets
Fixed assets are stated at cost, less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is provided using

the straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the assets, ranging from 4 years to
40 years. Depreciation expense totaled $240,477 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

Fixed assets (continued)

The Partnership evaluates long-lived assets held and used by the Partnership for impairment
whenever events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of the asset
may not be recoverable. An impairment loss is recognized if the sum of the expected
undiscounted future cash flows from the use and disposition of the asset is less than its
carrying amount. Generally, the amount of impairment loss is measured as the difference
between the carrying amount of the asset and the estimated fair value of the asset. The
Partnership did not record an impairment loss during the year ended December 31, 2020.

Debt issuance costs
Debt issuance costs are being amortized over the term of related mortgage note obligation
using the straight-line method, which approximates the effective interest method.

Amortization totaled $1,585 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

Profits, losses and distributions

Under the terms of the partnership agreement, profits and losses from operations are allocated
1% to the general partner and 99% to the limited partner. Cash distributions to the partners
are governed primarily by the regulatory agreement between the Partnership and HUD and
secondarily by the partnership agreement.

Income taxes

The accompanying financial statements do not reflect any provision for Partnership federal or
state income taxes since the Partnership’s profit or loss is reported by the partners on their
income tax returns. In accordance with Accounting Standards Codification (‘ASC’) 740,
Income Taxes, the Partnership applies the “more likely than not” threshold to the recognition
and derecognition of tax positions for its financial statements. Management has evaluated the
Partnership’s tax positions and has concluded that there wete no uncertain tax positions that
qualified for either recognition or disclosure in these financial statements.

In 2019, the State of Rhode Island enacted House Bill 5151, which established a new tax on

pass-through entities operating in the state. The Partnership incurred and paid state income
taxes of $18,000 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

SUMMARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES (CONTINUED)

Revenue recognition

Revenue is measured based on consideration specified in a contract with a customer, and
excludes any amounts collected on behalf of third parties. The Partnership recognizes revenue
when it satisfies a performance obligation by transferring control over a product or service to
a customer. The majority of the Partnership’s revenue originates from contracts with
customers to provide various healthcare services. The majority of the Partnership’s services
represent a bundle of services that are not capable of being distinct and as such, are treated as
a single performance obligation that is satisfied over time as the services are rendered.

The Partnership’s standard payment terms are within 30 days from billing.

‘The Partnership determines the transaction price based on contractually agreed upon rates,
adjusted for estimates of variable consideration, such as implicit price concessions. Variable
consideration also exists as the Partnership’s third-party revenue is paid principally at
prospectively determined rates. Retroactive adjustments are considered in the recognition of
revenue on an estimated basis in the period the related services are rendered such that net
patient service revenues are only recorded to the extent that it is probable that a significant
reversal in the amount of cumulative revenue recognized will not occur in the future. Any
differences between the estimated amounts accrued, and interim and final settlements are
adjusted in future periods as adjustments become known or as years are no longer subject to
such audits, reviews and investigations.

Disageregation of revenues

The Partnership operates as a skilled nursing facility and provides services to patients,
principally from Rhode Island, who have third-party financial coverage (principally Rhode
Tsland Medicaid and Medicare), as well as to other patients who are responsible for their own
financial obligations. Therefore, the Partnership’s viability is dependent on a number of factors
such as licensed bed capacity, occupancy rates, mix of patient by payer and case type, the rates
of reimbursement, changes to Medicaid and Medicare programs, and the Partnership’s ability
to collect on its contracts. All of the Partnership’s net patient service revenue for financial
reporting purposes are recorded over time as the services are rendered.

Net patient service revenue from third-party payers totaled $7,040,534 for the year ended

December 31, 2020. Net patient service revenue from private payers totaled $1,552,171 for
the year ended December 31, 2020.

Significant risks and uncertainties

Laws and regulations governing Medicare, Medicaid and other governmental reimbursement
programs are extremely complex and subject to interpretation. As a result, there is at least a
reasonable possibility that recorded estimates could change by a material amount in the near
term. It is management’s opinion that the Partnership is in compliance with applicable laws
and regulations; however, the possibility of government review and interpretation exists.
Compliance with such laws and regulations can be subject to future government review and
interpretation, as well as significant regulatory action; failure to comply with such laws and
regulations can result in fines, penalties and exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid programs.

‘Third-party advances

The Partnership records advances from third-party payors as a liability upon receipt.

Estimated amounts due to third-party payors

Estimated amounts due to third-party payors are principally related to third-party payments in
excess of outstanding balances which are finalized annually after the calendar year-end
concludes, and are typically received or funded by the end of the following calendar year.

Prepaid income, unearned CARES Act Funds

The Partnership records unearned Coronavirus Aid, Relief and Economic Security
(“CARES”) Act funds as a liability upon receipt and will recognize these funds as income
when the Partnership incurs qualifying expenses or lost revenue based on the Department of
Health and Human Services (“HHS”) terms and conditions associated with these funds.

Self-insurance costs
It is the Partnership’s policy to fund workers’ compensation and health care self-insurance

costs accrued. ‘The provision for such costs includes estimates of the ultimate costs for both
reported claims and claims incurred but not reported.

Subsequent events
The Partnership has evaluated subsequent events through June 23, 2021, the date that the

accompanying financial statements were available to be issued. Except as discussed in Notes
5 and 6, there were no material events that required recognition or additional disclosute.

OTHER LOAN AND NOTES PAYABLE AND SUBSEQUENT EVENT

On April 20, 2020, the Partnership received a loan in the amount of $1,183,000 under the
Paycheck Protection Program ("PPP") with its bank as part of the Small Business Act (“SBA”).
‘The PPP, which was established as part of the CARES Act, provides for loans to qualifying
businesses for amounts up to 2.5 times certain average monthly payroll expenses of the
qualifying business. The loans and accrued interest, or a portion thereof, may be forgiven after
twenty-four weeks so long as the borrower uses the loan proceeds for eligible purposes,
including payroll, benefits, rent, mortgage interest, and utilities, and maintains its payroil levels.
Not more than 40% of the amount forgiven can be attributable to non-payroll costs. The PPP
loan will be deferred until the SBA remits the loan forgiveness, if applicable, to the lender.

‘The Partnership currently intends to use the proceeds for purposes consistent with the PPP,
however, there can be no assurances that the Partnership will ultimately meet the conditions
for forgiveness of the loan or that the Partnership will not take actions that could cause the
Partnership to be ineligible for forgiveness of the loan, in whole or in part.

OTHER LOAN AND NOTES PAYABLE AND SUBSEQUENT EVENT
CONTINUED

U.S. GAAP does not contain authoritative accounting standards for forgivable loans provided
by governmental entities to a for profit entity. Absent authoritative accounting standards,
interpretative guidance issued and commonly applied by financial statement preparers allow
for the selection of accounting policies amongst acceptable alternatives. Based on the facts
and circumstances, the Partnership has determined it most appropriate to account for the PPP
loan proceeds under the debt model. The Partnership deemed the debt model to be the most
appropriate accounting policy for this arrangement as the underlying PPP loan is a legal form
of debt and there are significant contingencies outside of the control of the Partnership, mainly
related to the third-party approval process for forgiveness. Under the debt model, the
Partnership recognizes the proceeds received as debt, recognizes periodic interest expense in
the period in which the interest acctues at the stated interest rate and defers recognition of any
potential forgiveness of the loan principal or interest until the period in which the Partnership
has been legally released for its obligation by the lender. Accrued interest and principal
payments on the loan will commence, at a maximum, 10 months after the end of the 24-week
covered period if the loan has not been forgiven in full. The loan matures two years from the
date of first disbursement of proceeds to the Partnership. If the PPP loan if not forgiven, the
note accrues interest from the date of disbursement at 1%.

As of the date of this report, the PPP loan forgiveness has not been finalized. There can be
no assurance given that the Partnership will obtain forgiveness of the PPP Loan in whole or
in part. In order to apply for the PPP Loan, the Partnership certified that, among other things,
the current economic uncertainty made the PPP Loan request necessary to support its ongoing
operations. In addition, PPP loans under the CARES Act may be subject to certain rules,
regulations and procedures applicable to the SBA Loan Program, which includes PPP loans
under the CARES Act. The interpretation and applicability of these rules, regulations and
procedures is unclear, as some of them have not been referenced in the CARES Act itself or
in the guidance and interpretations issued by the SBA to date. If it is determined that the
Partnership was not eligible to receive the PPP Loan, or that the Partnership has not
adequately complied with the rules, regulations and procedures applicable to the SBA’s Loan
Program, the Partnership could be subject to penalties and could be required to repay the PPP
Loan in its entirety.

UNCERTAINTY DUE TO COVID-19

In March 2020, the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak to
constitute a “Public Health Emergency of International Concern.” Disruptions to the
Partnership’s business operations occurred during 2020 and continue into 2021 as a result
from the supply and quarantine of employees, residents, and vendors. ‘The Partnership, along
with most skilled nursing facilities throughout the U.S., has experienced a significant decline
in admissions and census and additional costs associated with retaining and attracting staff and
protective medical supplies due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Given the uncertainty of the
situation, an estimate of the financial impact to the Partnership, if any, cannot be reasonably
estimated at this time.

RELATED-PARTY TRANSACTIONS

Management fee

The Partnership has a management agreement with Health Concepts, Ltd. (the “Home
Office”), a company owned by the general partner, to provide home office services, principaily
management services. The agreement expires in May 2032, unless automatically renewed for
an additional 15-year term in December 2031. The HUD-approved management fee is a
maximum of 7% of net patient service revenue. Management fees totaled 7% of net patient
service revenue, and amounted to $601,489 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

Workers’ compensation insurance

Effective January 1, 1994, the Home Office received permission from the Rhode Island
Department of Labor to establish a pooled self-insured workers’ compensation plan (the
“Plan”). The Home Office, the Partnership and eight nursing facilities owned by the
Partnership’s general partner participate in the Pian and have transferred their workers’
compensation insurance to the Plan.

The Plan provides for the payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as
well as payment for losses. Each participant makes monthly contributions (premium
payments), as required, to the Health Concepts, Ltd. Workers’ Compensation Trust (the
“Trust”) through the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to establish a
cumulative reserve for future claims. The reserve is held in trust and invested by the Plan
trustee. The Trust carries excess liability insurance coverage with a commercial insurance
cartier to protect the Trust’s assets from individual losses in excess of $450,000. In addition,
the Trust carries a $1,000,000 bond in favor of Rhode Island Department of Labor,
collateralized by a $200,000 standby letter of credit with a bank, for which no amounts are
outstanding at December 31, 2020.

The Trust Committee (the “Committee”) maintains separate accountability for cach
participant’s portion of contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for future
claims. Should any participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs and
losses, the remaining participants’ portion of the Trust assets can be used to satisfy the
payments allocated to that participant. In the event of Plan termination, any assets remaining
in the [rust in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will ultimately be
returned to the participants based on their pro rata shares.

In the opinion of the Committee, the Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion
of current and estimated future costs, losses and future claims; accordingly, the Partnership’s
required premium for the year ended December 31, 2020, totaied $137,680, an amount that,
in management’s opinion, is below the premium it would pay to a commercial insurance cartier
if the Plan did not exist and did not achieve significant savings as a result of the loss control
program and monitoring services provided by the Home Office.

Defined contribution plan

age 18 and the completion of more than 999 hours of service in a prior year.

For 2020, the plan provides that the Partnership will match 75% of employee contributions
up to a maximum match of 7.5% of eligible compensation. The Partnership’s contributions
to the plan totaled $188,732 for the year ended December 31, 2020.

Health insurance

Effective January 1, 2018, the Home Office established a self-insured health insurance plan
(the “Health Plan”). ‘The Home Office, the Partnership and other nursing facilities and a
business owned by the Partnership’s general partner participate in the Health Plan and have
transfetred their health insurance to the Health Plan. The Health Plan provides for the
payment of administration, claims and risk management costs, as well as payment for losses.
Fach participant makes monthly contributions (premium payments), as required, to the Health
Plan account maintained at the Home Office to pay current costs and losses and to establish
a cumulative reserve for future claims.

The Health Plan carries excess loss insurance coverage with a commercial insurance carrier to
8 -
protect the Health Plan’s assets from individual losses in excess of $100,000.

‘The Home Office maintains separate accountability for each participant’s portion of
contributions, costs, incurred losses and cumulative reserve for future claims. Should any
participant’s premiums be inadequate for its share of claims, costs, and losses, the remaining
participants’ portion of Health Pian assets can be used to satisfy the payments allocated to that
participant. In the event of Health Plan termination, any assets remaining in the Health Plan
in excess of amounts needed to pay claims, costs and losses will ultimately be returned to the
patticipants based on their pro rata shares. In the opinion of the Home Office, the Health
Plan has sufficient assets to meet a significant portion of current and estimated future costs,
losses and future claims; the Partnership’s expense for the year ended December 31, 2020,
totaled $616,486.

MEDICAID ELIGIBILITY DETERMINATION DELAYS AND COMMITMENT

Medicaid eligibility determination delays

Since early 2016, the State has been significantly delayed in rendering Medicaid eligibility
determinations with respect to patients that the Partnership has determined should be eligible
for Medicaid and for whom a completed application for Medicaid benefits has been filed with
the State. The Partnership provides services to these patients and recognizes related revenue
during the period in which the State has not made a determination related to a completed
application filed with the State (“Medicaid Pending Application”). Amounts reported as
tenant accounts receivable related to Medicaid Pending Applications that have been pending
for less than 90 days and those that have been pending for 90 days or more for which the
Partnership has not requested an advance payment (see Note 2) may be subject to subsequent
denial by the State at some future date. Management believes that the State will ultimately
determine that patients for whom a Medicaid Pending Application exists are eligible for
Medicaid and that any potential loss related to Medicaid Pending Applications subsequently
denied by the State will not have a material adverse effect on the Partnership’s financial
position.

Commitment

In a prior year, the Partnership was a party to a settlement agreement with the United States
Department of Justice, Office of Inspector General (“OIG”), in which the Partnership paid
an agreed-upon balance relating to previously submitted therapy claims for the period
January 1, 2010 through December 31, 2015. In addition, as part of the settlement agreement,
the Partnership became a patty to a Corporate Integrity Agreement (“CIA”) with the OIG.
The CIA requites that the Home Office establish and maintain a Compliance Program that
promotes adherence with Medicare and Medicaid regulations for all skilled nursing facilities
affiliated with or owned, operated or managed by the Home Office, including the Partnership.
The CIA is for a five-year period commencing September 2016. During the years ended
December 31, 2017 and 2018, and in January 2020 and January 2021, the OIG accepted the
Annual Reports submitted by the Home Office pursuant to the CIA. The Home Office is
compliant with the requirements of the CIA as of December 31, 2020.

To the Partners

Westerly Health Center Associates, L.P.
(a Limited Partnership)

Westerly, Rhode Island

We have audited, in accordance with auditing standards generally accepted in the United States of America
and the standards applicable to financial audits contained in Government Auditing Standards issued by the
Comptroller General of the United States, the financial statements of Westerly Health Center Associates, L.P.
(a Limited Partnership) (the “Partnership”), which comprise the balance sheet as of December 31, 2020, and
the related statements of loss, partners’ equity and cash flows for the year then ended, and the related notes
to the financial statements, and have issued our report thereon dated June 23, 2021.

Internal Control over Financial Reporting

Tn planning and performing our audit of the financial statements, we considered the Partnership’s internal
control over financial reporting (internal control) as a basis for designing audit procedures that are appropriate
in the circumstances for the purpose of expressing our opinion on the financial statements, but not for the
purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of the Partnership’s internal control. Accordingly, we
do not express an opinion on the effectiveness of the Partnership’s internal control.

A deficiency in internal control exists when the design or operation of a contro] does not allow management or
employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to prevent, or detect and correct,
misstatements on a timely basis. A material weakness is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencics, in internal
control, such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the entity’s financial
statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected on a timely basis. A significant deficiency is a
deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in internal control that is less severe than a material weakness,
yet important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance.

Our consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described in the first paragraph of this
section and was not designed to identify all deficiencies in internal control that might be material weaknesses
or significant deficiencies. Given these limitations, during our audit we did not identify any deficiencies in
internal control that we consider to be material weaknesses. However, material weaknesses may exist that
have not been identified.

Report on Internal Control over Compliance

Management of the Partnership is responsible for establishing and maintaining effective internal control over
compliance with the compliance requirements referred to above. In planning and performing our audit of
compliance, we considered the Pattnership’s internal control over compliance with the requirements that
could have a direct and material effect on its major HUD program to determine the auditing procedures that
ate appropriate in the circumstances for the purpose of expressing an opinion on compliance for its major
HUD program and to test and report on internal control over compliance in accordance with the audit guide,
but not for the purpose of expressing an opinion on the effectiveness of internal control over compliance.
Accordingly, we do not express an opinion on the effectiveness of the Partnership’s internal control over
compliance.

A deficiency in internal control over compliance exists when the design or operation of a control over compliance
does not allow management or employees, in the normal course of performing their assigned functions, to
prevent, or detect and correct, noncompliance with a compliance requirement of a HUD program on a timely
basis. A material weakness in internal control over compliance is a deficiency, or combination of deficiencies, in internal
control over compliance, such that there is a reasonable possibility that material noncompliance with a
compliance requirement of a HUD program will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely
basis. A significant deficiency in internal control over compliance is a deficiency, or a combination of deficiencies, in
internal control over compliance with a compliance requirement of a HUD program that is less severe than a
material weakness in internal control over compliance, yet important enough to merit attention by those
charged with governance.

To whom it may concern:

We submit the following letter in connection with the Entities Listed in Appendix A’s (the “Applicant”) application
for a Change in Effective Control of the Entities listed in Appendix B (the “Acquired Entities”) (the “Application”). The
financial information provided to you and compiled by the Applicant as Tab 28 in the Application accurately
presents the financial condition and results of operations of the Entities Listed in Appendix C (the “Holding
Entities”) from the Holding Entities’ inception in 2019 until June 30, 2021. The Holding Entities currently
own eight (8) skilled nursing facilities (the “Facilities”), four (4) of which were purchased in 2019 and four
(4) of which were purchased in 2020. The Facilities are independently operated and managed by
experienced facility-employed administrators. More specifically, Tab 28 includes the following financial
information for each of the Holding Entities:

       •    Pages 1 and 2 present the property values and mortgage balances of each of the Holding
            Entities. The total property values of the Holding Entities’ proportional ownership in the
            Applicant is $176.2 million and the total mortgage balance is $87.2 million.

       •    Page 3 presents the annualized cash flow for the Holding Entities proportional ownership
            interest in the Applicant, totaling approximately $15.1 million.

       •    Page 4 presents the balance sheet of the proportional interest of the Holding Entities, which
            presents total equity of approximately $126.6 million.

In evaluating the Applicant’s financial condition, the cash flows presented in Tab 28 show the Entities’
ability to earn income from the Facilities, and the balance sheets show the significant investment made
in the Facilities.

Additionally, as highlighted in Question 1 of the Application, the Facilities are affiliated with sister
companies, that when combined, consists of a portfolio of thirty-one (33) skilled nursing facilities, also
independently operated and managed, and which have a proven history of providing high quality long-term care services.
Gorfine, Schiller & Gardyn, P.A. currently audits the financial statements of sixteen (16) of these skilled
nursing facility affiliates and prepares their tax returns. The Applicant and its affiliates are third-generation
operators in the nursing home industry and have demonstrated the ability to purchase struggling nursing
homes and make the changes necessary to operate them profitably and successfully. The Applicant and
its affiliates also have the banking and industry relationships needed to ensure success.

Based on the financial information provided in Tab 28 of the Application, and the relationship between
the Applicant and the larger portfolio’s successful skilled nursing facility affiliates, and the certified audits
we have conducted on behalf of the portfolio entities, we certify that in our professional opinion, the
Holding Entities have the financial ability to consummate the purchase of the Acquired Entities and to
successfully continue the operations of the Acquired Entities.




Gorfine, Schiller & Gardyn, P.A.
